testCases.input: How do n-gram embedding tables compare to traditional embeddings in enhancing language model performance?
testCases.actualOutput:
The paper "Low-Bit N-Gram Embeddings for Language Models" (arXiv:2610.31646v1) highlights significant advantages of n-gram embedding tables over traditional embeddings in enhancing language model performance. Specifically, the authors note that using n-gram embeddings—particularly bigrams and trigrams—improves language modeling performance compared to models that do not utilize these tables.

In their methodology, the authors employ four embedding tables (two for bigrams and two for trigrams) that are learned jointly with the language model. This approach allows the model to retrieve embeddings that capture different context patterns, which is crucial for effective language modeling. The paper states, "Previous work has shown that this method improves language modeling performance, with further gains as the number of embeddings increases" [2].

Moreover, the study demonstrates that even when compressing these n-gram tables to low-bit precision, the performance benefits are largely retained. For instance, four-bit tables save approximately 75% of table memory while preserving more than 99% of the improvement provided by full-precision tables. In contrast, traditional embeddings do not exhibit the same level of efficiency or performance retention when subjected to similar compression techniques [1][4].

Overall, the findings suggest that n-gram embedding tables not only enhance performance but also allow for significant memory savings, making them a more efficient choice compared to traditional embeddings in language models. This efficiency is further underscored by the ability to reinvest saved memory into additional embeddings, potentially leading to even better performance [1].
testCases.expectedOutput: N-gram embedding tables enhance language model performance by storing learned representations of short token sequences, such as pairs or triples of consecutive tokens. This approach allows models to retrieve relevant embeddings during processing, adding substantial capacity with minimal computational overhead. In contrast, traditional embeddings typically represent individual tokens without capturing their contextual relationships as effectively. Studies show that n-gram tables can significantly improve performance, with low-bit precision methods preserving most of these benefits while reducing memory costs. For instance, three-bit n-gram tables can save approximately 75% of table memory while retaining over 99% of the validation-loss improvement compared to models without n-gram embeddings.

Low-Bit N-Gram Embeddings for Language Models

Section: 5 Conclusion

We propose low-bit precision for n-gram embedding tables and systematically study its effects on memory use and model performance. Across models trained from scratch, four-bit tables save approximately 75% of table memory while preserving more than 99% of the improvement provided by full-precision tables. Choosing appropriate embedding scales matters more than the choice of codebook, and mixed precision allows different n-gram tables to use the precision they need. At lower precision, a brief fine-tuning phase can recover much of the lost performance. These findings also extend to DeepSeek-V4.1-Flash and Qwen3.8-Flash-Next, where compression saves 47-55% of table memory with little change in perplexity and downstream performance. Beyond reducing memory use, reinvesting the savings in more embeddings can improve performance over the original full-precision tables. Together, our results offer practical guidance for making n-gram memory more efficient and using the saved capacity to build better language models.

Low-Bit N-Gram Embeddings for Language Models

Section: 2 Method

N-gram embedding tables. Following the Over-Tokenized Transformer [1], we use four embedding tables: two for bigrams and two for trigrams, as illustrated in Figure 1. The embeddings in these tables are learned jointly with the language model, with one embedding stored in each row. At each token position, the bigram and trigram ending at the current token each retrieve one embedding from each of their two corresponding tables. These four embeddings are then concatenated and added to the token embedding. Previous work has shown that this method improves language modeling performance, with further gains as the number of embeddings increases [1].
2
Low-Bit N-Gram Embeddings for Language Models
Formally, let x t denote the current token, E the token embedding matrix with embedding dimension d , and T 1 , . . . , T 4 the four tables. We construct the model input as
where n 1 = n 2 = 2 for the bigram tables and n 3 = n 4 = 3 for the trigram tables. Here, the hash function h j determines which embedding is retrieved by mapping the token sequence to an address in table T j . These retrieved embeddings each have dimension d/ 4, so concatenating all four gives the same dimension as E [ x t ].
Low-bit embeddings. We propose reducing the memory cost of these trained tables by storing their embeddings at low precision. To do this, we give each table a set of up to 2 b representative values, commonly called a codebook , and represent each embedding component by a b -bit index into these shared codebook values. To account for differences in magnitude between embeddings, we also store one 16-bit scale per embedding. During reconstruction, the index selects a codebook value, which is then multiplied by the embedding's scale. Thus, the original component w ri at position i of embedding r is reconstructed as
where s r is the scale, c k is codebook value k , and q ri is the stored index (Figure 1b).
This low-bit representation substantially reduces table memory. For an embedding with p components, memory use falls from 16 p bits to pb + 16 bits. For instance, with p = 128, two-bit precision reduces the memory required per embedding by approximately 87%, from 2,048 to 272 bits.
However, bigram and trigram embeddings represent different context patterns, so they may need different precision to preserve their contribution to model performance. We therefore propose using a mixture of bit widths across the two n-gram orders, allocating more bits to the tables that are more sensitive to quantization within a fixed table memory budget.
Choosing the codebook values. We consider three codebook families. First, uniform codebooks use equally spaced values. For instance, at two bits, the codebook values are {-1 , -1 / 3 , 1 / 3 , 1 } . We also test a variant that includes zero, using {-1 , 0 , 1 } , so that zero can be represented exactly. Second, normal-quantile codebooks take values from quantiles of a standard normal distribution, placing more of them near zero. Third, we learn the codebook values from each table's trained embeddings using Lloyd-Max quantization [4, 5].
To learn the Lloyd-Max codebook, we first normalize each embedding by its root mean square, allowing embeddings of different magnitudes to share a codebook. We initialize the codebook values at quantiles of the normalized components, then repeatedly assign components to their nearest codebook value and replace each value with the mean of its assigned components. This fitting runs once during compression, using only the trained embeddings. Appendix A.2 gives the implementation details.
Choosing the embedding scales. Once the codebook values are fixed, we consider three ways to choose each embedding's scale s r . First, maximum-based scaling matches the largest absolute codebook value to the embedding's largest absolute component. Second, root-mean-square (RMS) scaling uses the embedding's overall magnitude, calculated as s r = √ 1 p ∑ i w 2 ri . Third, error-fitted scaling chooses the scale to minimize the mean squared error between the original embedding and its reconstruction. We compare these choices to examine how scale selection affects compression quality.
After determining the codebook values and embedding scales, we store them together with the low-bit indices in place of the original embedding tables. During inference, the model retrieves embeddings from this stored representation without repeating the fitting procedure.

Low-Bit N-Gram Embeddings for Language Models

Low-Bit N-Gram Embeddings for Language Models

Section: C.6 Alternative hashing methods

To examine whether the way n-grams share embedding parameters affects low-bit performance, we compare conventional whole-embedding hashing with two component-wise alternatives. Conventional hashing maps an n-gram to one embedding in each table and retrieves all its components together. Consequently, two n-grams mapped to the same embedding share every component. The alternatives instead choose a separate address for each output component while keeping the same table size and embedding dimension.
Same-column hashing. We retain the table as a matrix, with one embedding per row and one component per column. To construct component j of an n-gram embedding, we hash the n-gram together with j to choose a row, then retrieve the value in column j of that row. Different components can therefore come from different embeddings, but the first component always comes from the first column, the second from the second column, and so on.
Fully random component hashing. We flatten the same table into a vector and hash the n-gram together with each component index to select a value anywhere in that vector. Unlike same-column hashing, the selected value can come from any column as well as any row. In both variants, the hash addresses are fixed: the same n-gram always retrieves the same components, whose values are learned during training.
Experimental setup. We compare all three methods on nanochat 26M, GPT-2-family 30M, and Llamafamily 31M, using the default 262k embeddings per table, ClimbMix, and three seeds. Each comparison uses the same training setup and evaluates both 16-bit and two-bit tables. The two-bit models use quantized embeddings throughout pre-training, following Appendix B.4. We quantize each table using Lloyd-Max codebooks and error-fitted scales before gathering its components, so each selected component keeps the scale of its source embedding.
Table 10: Alternative hashing methods at 16-bit and two-bit precision. Values give the improvement relative to conventional 16-bit tables (%), reported as mean ± sample standard deviation over three seeds. For every row, 100% denotes the validation-loss reduction from adding conventional 16-bit tables to the corresponding model without tables.
Discussion. Table 10 shows that both component-wise methods improve the average two-bit result over conventional hashing on all three architectures. Their improvement reaches 93.6-100.3% of that provided by conventional 16-bit tables, compared with 87.0-93.7% for conventional two-bit hashing. The gains are larger on GPT-2 and Llama than on nanochat, suggesting that the choice of shared embedding components can help preserve performance at low precision.
Same-column hashing also appears promising beyond low precision. It improves mean performance over conventional hashing in five of the six settings, including two of the three full-precision comparisons. One possible explanation is that component-wise hashing allows n-grams to share individual components without sharing an entire embedding, reducing interference from whole-embedding collisions. These results suggest that same-column hashing may offer broader benefits for language modeling. Establishing how consistently it helps and whether collision patterns explain these gains deserves further investigation beyond the scope of this study, which focuses on low-precision embeddings.
24

Low-Bit N-Gram Embeddings for Language Models

Section: 3.2 Table memory savings and model performance

We first ask how much table memory can be removed before the model loses the benefit of n-gram embeddings. We compress the trained tables to one through four bits using Lloyd-Max codebooks with fitted scales. To test whether larger tables can tolerate the same compression, we also increase the number of embeddings per table from the default 262k to 1M in the 26M nanochat model and both Llama-family models.
The results are shown in Figure 2. We find that low-bit compression retains most of the improvement at three or four bits. For example, four-bit tables save 74-75% of table memory while retaining more than 99% of the original improvement. However, reducing precision further hurts performance. Two-bit tables save 86-87% of table memory but retain only 85.9-91.0% of the original improvement. Appendix C gives the full results, including one-bit compression.

Low-Bit N-Gram Embeddings for Language Models

Section: 3.1 Experimental setup

Models and data. We train five language models from scratch: nanochat with 26M and 50M parameters, a GPT-2-family model with 30M parameters, and Llama-family models with 31M and 322M parameters. By default, each model uses four n-gram tables, comprising two bigram and two trigram tables, with approximately 262k embeddings per table. We train on ClimbMix [10] and repeat each experiment with three random seeds. Appendix B.1 gives the model configurations and training settings.
Evaluation. For each model, we first train two versions using the same experimental setup, one with fullprecision (16-bit) n-gram tables and one without tables. We evaluate both on a held-out validation dataset, and their difference in validation loss measures the improvement from adding the tables. We then reduce the precision of the trained tables and evaluate the model again to measure how much of this improvement remains. We report this as the percentage of the original improvement retained, where 100% matches the full-precision tables and 0% matches the model trained without tables. Alongside this performance measure, we report the percentage of table memory saved. Results are averaged over three seeds, with standard deviations where shown.

Low-bit n-gram embeddings significantly enhance memory efficiency while retaining a substantial portion of performance compared to full precision. The research presented in "Low-Bit N-Gram Embeddings for Language Models" (arXiv:2610.31646v1) demonstrates that using four-bit tables can save approximately 75% of table memory while preserving over 99% of the performance improvement associated with full-precision tables. In contrast, further reductions in precision, such as two-bit tables, can lead to memory savings of 86-87%, but at the cost of retaining only 85.9-91.0% of the original performance benefits.

The study highlights that the choice of embedding scales is crucial, with mixed precision allowing different n-gram tables to utilize the precision they require. Notably, a brief fine-tuning phase after compression can recover much of the performance lost due to low-bit embeddings. For instance, after fine-tuning, one- and two-bit tables retained 65.3% and 92.0% of the improvement provided by full-precision tables, respectively. Overall, the findings suggest that low-bit n-gram embeddings not only reduce memory requirements but also allow for the potential reinvestment of saved memory into additional embeddings, which can enhance performance beyond that of the original full-precision tables while still using less memory [1][2][3][4].

Together, our results offer practical guidance for making n-gram memory more efficient and using the saved capacity to build better language models.

Low-Bit N-Gram Embeddings for Language Models

Section: 3.2 Table memory savings and model performance

We first ask how much table memory can be removed before the model loses the benefit of n-gram embeddings. We compress the trained tables to one through four bits using Lloyd-Max codebooks with fitted scales. To test whether larger tables can tolerate the same compression, we also increase the number of embeddings per table from the default 262k to 1M in the 26M nanochat model and both Llama-family models.
The results are shown in Figure 2. We find that low-bit compression retains most of the improvement at three or four bits. For example, four-bit tables save 74-75% of table memory while retaining more than 99% of the original improvement. However, reducing precision further hurts performance. Two-bit tables save 86-87% of table memory but retain only 85.9-91.0% of the original improvement. Appendix C gives the full results, including one-bit compression.

Low-Bit N-Gram Embeddings for Language Models

Section: 3.5 Recovering performance with low-bit training

Compressing the n-gram tables changes the embeddings that the model learned to use, which can reduce performance. We therefore ask whether a short fine-tuning phase can recover this loss, or whether using low-bit embeddings throughout pre-training is more effective. To train with low-bit embeddings, we maintain a BF16 copy for gradient updates but quantize the retrieved embeddings during each forward pass. Both the embeddings and the rest of the model remain trainable, allowing the model to adapt to the chosen precision. We compare four sequences: (1) compress → pre-train, (2) pre-train → compress →fi ne-tune, (3) pre-train → fi ne-tune → compress, and (4) pre-train → compress. Comparing fine-tuning before and after compression tests whether recovery comes from adapting to low-bit embeddings rather than simply receiving more training.
The results are summarized in Figure 6. We observe that a brief fine-tuning phase after compression recovers much of the performance lost at very low precision. After fine-tuning, one- and two-bit tables retain 65.3% and 92.0% of the improvement provided by full-precision tables, respectively. Surprisingly, one-bit embeddings perform even better when used throughout pre-training, retaining 77.0% of the full-precision tables' improvement. This shows that even one bit per embedding component can preserve a large share of the benefit from n-gram tables when the model learns to use them from the start. Appendix C.5 gives the full results, while Appendix C.6 examines how alternative hashing methods affect performance with low-bit embeddings.

Low-Bit N-Gram Embeddings for Language Models

Abstract: Many recent open-weight language models use n-gram embedding tables to improve performance. These tables store learned representations of short token sequences, such as pairs or triples of consecutive tokens, which the model retrieves during processing. However, they can require substantial memory: DeepSeek-V4.1-Flash, for example, allocates 196 billion parameters to its Engram n-gram memory. We therefore investigate whether this memory cost can be reduced while preserving the performance improvement that the tables provide. We propose storing n-gram embeddings at low precision and systematically investigate different quantization methods and bit allocations across tables. Across nanochat-, Llama-, and GPT-2-family models trained from scratch, four-bit tables save approximately 75% of table memory while preserving more than 99% of the validation-loss improvement from adding the tables. Using fewer bits leads to a larger drop in performance, although we find that a short fine-tuning phase recovers a significant part of this loss. In addition, reinvesting the saved memory in larger tables can improve performance beyond that of the original full-precision tables while still using less memory. These table memory savings also extend to large existing models: on DeepSeek-V4.1-Flash and Qwen3.8-Flash-Next, low-bit tables save 47-55% of table memory, with perplexity increases of less than 1.2% and largely preserved downstream task performance. These findings establish low-bit precision as a practical way to reduce the memory requirements of n-gram embeddings and use the saved capacity to improve model performance.

Section: Low-Bit N-Gram Embeddings for Language Models

Stephen Chung
Wenyu Du

Low-Bit N-Gram Embeddings for Language Models

Section: 1 Introduction

Recent studies have shown that n-gram embedding tables can improve language model performance with little additional computation [1, 2]. These tables store learned representations of short token sequences, such as pairs or triples of consecutive tokens. At each position, the model retrieves the corresponding representations to supplement its processing of the text. Because each lookup accesses only a few embeddings, the tables can add substantial model capacity while keeping the computation per token small. This approach has been adopted in DeepSeek's Engram memory, which contains 196 billion parameters in DeepSeek-V4.1-Flash [3]. However, storing these large tables requires substantial memory, motivating methods that preserve their performance benefits with a smaller memory footprint.
The memory cost arises from the enormous number of possible token combinations. To accommodate them, existing methods map n-grams into a fixed number of table embeddings, allowing multiple n-grams to share the same embedding [1, 2]. Smaller tables force more unrelated sequences to share representations, which can reduce their benefit to the model. Increasing the number of embeddings alleviates this problem but requires more memory. We therefore investigate a different way to reduce table memory: keeping the embeddings while using fewer bits for each embedding value. This also raises an opportunity: if lower precision preserves most of the tables' benefit, the saved memory could support more embeddings and ultimately improve performance.
We propose compressing n-gram embedding tables by storing each value at low precision. At such low precision, the choice of representable values can affect how well the embeddings are preserved. We therefore systematically compare evenly spaced values, values chosen from normal quantiles, and values fitted to the learned embedding distribution using Lloyd-Max quantization [4, 5]. We also examine whether bigram and trigram tables benefit from different precision levels, allowing us to allocate bits according to their sensitivity to compression. Together, these experiments offer practical guidance on choosing quantization methods and bit allocations to balance table memory and model performance.

We evaluate this approach on nanochat-, Llama-, and GPT-2-family models trained from scratch [6-9]. We train each model with and without n-gram tables to establish how much the tables improve performance. We then compress the trained tables to different precisions and measure the table memory saved and the improvement retained. Beyond compression alone, we investigate whether a short fine-tuning phase can recover lost performance and whether reinvesting the saved memory in additional embeddings can outperform the original full-precision tables. To test whether these savings extend to large existing models, we also compress the tables in DeepSeek-V4.1-Flash and Qwen3.8-Flash-Next, saving 47-55% of table memory while largely preserving performance on downstream tasks.
Our main contributions are:
Substantial table memory savings with little loss of performance. Across three model architectures, three-bit n-gram tables save 80% of table memory while retaining approximately 97% of the validation-loss improvement from adding the tables. We also demonstrate substantial table memory savings in DeepSeek-V4.1-Flash and Qwen3.8-Flash-Next.
Practical guidance on quantization and precision allocation. We systematically compare codebook construction, scale fitting, and precision allocation across bigram and trigram tables.
Performance recovery through fine-tuning. A short fine-tuning phase substantially reduces the performance loss from low-bit compression, making aggressive compression more effective.
Better performance by reinvesting saved memory. Tables with four times as many embeddings, stored at two bits, achieve 122-126% of the original tables' improvement while still using 46-48% less table memory. This shows that reducing precision can enable larger, more effective n-gram memories.

testCases.input: How do rVCs differ from bVCs in agent authentication, specifically in terms of roles, capabilities, and issuance authority?
testCases.actualOutput:
In the context of agent authentication, rich Verifiable Credentials (rVCs) and basic Verifiable Credentials (bVCs) serve distinct purposes and differ significantly in their content and issuance authority.

**Roles and Capabilities**: rVCs are designed to convey detailed identity attributes, including roles, capabilities, and authorizations of an agent. This allows agents to present comprehensive information about themselves during authentication processes. In contrast, bVCs are minimalistic and only encode basic information, such as the fact that the entity is an agent, without specifying any roles or capabilities. This fundamental difference means that while rVCs enable agents to assert their specific functionalities and permissions, bVCs do not provide such granularity and are primarily used for initial identification within a security domain.

**Issuance Authority**: The issuance of bVCs is restricted to the orchestrator of the security domain, which is responsible for equipping newly deployed agents with these basic credentials. This means that bVCs are only issued by a centralized authority within the domain. On the other hand, rVCs can be issued by designated authority agents within the same security domain during an intra-domain attestation process. This process involves mutual authentication where the requesting agent presents its bVC, and the issuing agent provides the rVC, thereby establishing a trust relationship based on more detailed identity claims.

In summary, rVCs provide a richer set of identity attributes and are issued through a more decentralized process compared to bVCs, which serve as a basic identification tool issued by a central authority within the security domain ([1. arXiv:2511.02841v2], [2. arXiv:2511.02841v2]).
testCases.expectedOutput: rVCs (rich Verifiable Credentials) differ from bVCs (basic Verifiable Credentials) in that rVCs specify additional identity attributes such as roles, capabilities, or authorizations of an agent, while bVCs only encode minimal information, primarily confirming that the entity is an agent without detailing its specific roles or capabilities. rVCs are issued by a designated authority agent within the same security domain, whereas bVCs are solely issued by the security domain's orchestrator. This distinction allows agents with rVCs to engage in more complex interactions and trust relationships compared to those with only bVCs.

VCs are explicitly allowed to carry claims in the form of unstructured data such as natural language text, images, or audio. Since modern LLM-based AI agents are able to produce and interpret unstructured content, they can issue and verify unstructured, schemaless claims about other agents. These novel types of claims can bootstrap automated and dynamic trust establishment in multi-agent and cross-domain ecosystems, as different domains do not need to go through an extensive standardization process to reach an agreement on a common rigid VC schema.

AI Agents with Decentralized Identifiers and Verifiable Credentials

Section: 4 Concept Within our concept, each agent lives in the realm of a security domain and is in control of its own DID and VCs. All agents of a security domain are deployed by a dedicated orchestrator. Each agent's DID is anchored in a jointly operated distributed ledger that spans multiple security domains. The ledger is considered to be commonly governed by participants originating from different security domains. It acts as a cross-domain trust anchor for DID docs. Only the agent in possession of the private key associated with a DID is authorized to update its ledger-anchored DID doc, while all agents of the same or different security domain are only allowed to read it. This design ensures tamper-resistant and cross-domain persistence of an agent's identifier and the associated verification material in the form of public keys. So as per definition, each agent has inherent confidence in the operation of the ledger. For secure handling of the agent DID's private key and the VCs themselves, every agent is equipped with a digital wallet. When initiating a dialogue, agents must mutually authenticate, regardless of whether they belong to the same or different security domains and regardless of the dialogue's purpose, e.g., attestation or service invocation. This zero trust-compliant approach requires each agent to prove ownership of its DID and to present supporting VCs to the other party. The VCs must be cryptographically bound to the DID under investigation. During this exchange, both agents alternate between the roles of a VC holder and a VP verifier: the holder presents its DID and VCs in the form of a VP, while the verifier checks the validity and issuer trustworthiness. If both parties approve the validity of each other's VPs, they are mutually authenticated respectively established trust among each other. At deployment, an agent receives basic (bVCs) or rich VCs (rVCs), depending on its initial role. bVCs encode only minimal information, such as the fact that the entity is an agent, without specifying roles, attributes, capabilities, or authorizations. They are only issued by the security domain's orchestrator. Hence, a bVC contains the orchestrator's DID as the issuer's identifier. While the orchestrator holds its own DID outside the ledger, its DID doc with its verification material is made available to all agents within its security domain. The purpose of bVCs is to empower freshly-deployed agents to trustfully identify themselves to peers of the same security domain in order to receive rVCs. The latter specify additional identity attributes such as roles, capabilities, or authorizations of an agent. Obtaining rVCs after deployment involves an intra-domain attestation process. For this, a freshly-deployed agent approaches a designated authority agent of the same security domain that is in charge to equip agents with rVCs. The attestation is then accomplished through a dialog where one acts as a rVC requester and the other as a rVC issuer. As a dialog requires mutual authentication, the requesting agent presents its bVCs, while the issuer presents its own rVCs. Once both sides are verified, the issuer creates and hands over the desired rVC, which the receiving agent then stores in its wallet for later use. The conceptual workflow and trust model for one security domain is illustrated in Figure 1. To get access to the ledger, each security domain is equipped with a dedicated instance of the DIF Universal Resolver 8 , which exposes a REST end point for tools to fetch DID docs. In the experimental setup, the publicly accessible BCovrin ledger 9 , operated by the Province of British Columbia, serves as the test ledger. It is based on the Hyperledger Indy technology 10 . As both security domains do not run nodes of the ledger, they are neither involved in its operation nor governance. The prototype's architecture is illustrated in Figure 2. In a security domain, a dedicated agent acts exclusively as an issuer of rVCs (identity issuer in Figure 2). For the attestation, the requesting agent is provisioned with a bVC, while the issuing agent is provisioned with rVCs at deployment time. The rVCs issued during attestation are then used by the agents to mutually authenticate in the cross-domain dialogue via the A2A protocol. The exchange of VPs required for mutual authentication, both at the start of the intradomain attestation process and in the cross-domain dialogue, is carried out using the DIF Presentation Exchange protocol. The attestation relies on the DIF Credential Manifest protocol 11 . 8 https://github.com/decentralized-identity/ universal-resolver 9 http://test.bcovrin.vonx.io/ 10 https://www.lfdecentralizedtrust.org/projects/ hyperledger-indy In the setup, each agent is instructed about its role through a system prompt for the LLM. The prompt describes, in natural language and from the agent's role perspective, the sequence of steps required for the intra-domain authentication and attestation, and inter-domain authentication dialogue. It thus specifies how the agent should proceed in order to achieve mutual authentication and attestation. Consequently, these security-critical procedures are not encoded in the deterministic part of the agent but are instead orchestrated by the LLM. This design decision is motivated by several factors. Decision-making authority for trust establishment was deliberately delegated to the LLM, as it is capable of interpreting and evaluating unstructured claims in VCs. Moreover, the use of system prompts allows for flexible, contextdependent modifications of the processes, such as reducing the authentication protocol to one-way authentication when situationally appropriate.

AI Agents with Decentralized Identifiers and Verifiable Credentials

Section: 2 Fundamentals

As introduced by the W3C, DIDs and VCs are central building blocks of the self-sovereign identity (SSI) paradigm (Toth and Anderson-Priddy, 2019). SSI
is an identity model that shifts control of identifiers and credentials from centralized authorities to the individuals that own them, enabling autonomy, privacy preservation, and selective disclosure of information. A DID is a unique, cryptographically verifiable identifier that resolves to a unique DID document (abbr. as DID doc), which specifies public keys, service endpoints, and authentication methods. Since the DID owner possesses the corresponding private keys, it can cryptographically prove ownership of the DID. To ensure integrity and global availability, DID docs are typically anchored in distributed ledgers or other decentralized infrastructures. VCs complement DIDs by enabling third parties to express claims in a signed, tamper-evident format about a subject. The latter is in the claim referred to by its DID. VCs are ideally stored locally by the claim's subject and are shared with others only on demand in the form of a Verifiable Presentation (VP), giving the subject finegrained control over disclosure. SSI defines three roles: issuers, who create, sign and issue VCs; holders and often referred to as the DID subjects, who control and selectively present them as VPs; and verifiers, who validate the integrity and authenticity of a given VP and the trustworthiness of the issuer of the contained VC. As autonomy and privacy-preservation become essential properties of agents operating across organizational boundaries, DIDs and VCs provide a robust foundation for secure, interoperable, and verifiable identity claims.
DIDs and VCs offer several advantages for agents. DID docs do not reveal the agent's identity since they contain no identity attributes. This makes them an ideal artifact to be shared via a commonly accessible ledger. Moreover, in combination with the latter, agents can securely and trustfully update the cryptographic binding of their DIDs to their public keys, e.g., to rotate keys for security purposes, without involving any issuer such as a certificate authority in conventional public key infrastructures. The concept also permits declaring deputies in the DID doc, which allows encoding and enforcing complex human-toagent and agent-to-agent owner relationships (Rodriguez Garzon et al., 2025). Furthermore, VCs are highly flexible and tamper-proof containers for a wide range of claims, making them suitable for carrying human-to-agent and agent-to-agent delegations.

AI Agents with Decentralized Identifiers and Verifiable Credentials

Section: 3 Related Work

Equipping agents with DIDs and VCs has recently attracted significant attention as a foundation for secure and privacy-preserving identity management in multi- agent ecosystems. Chaffer et al. (Chaffer et al., 2024) present the ETHOS framework, which adopts the SSI paradigm for agents. Their work highlights benefits in terms of privacy preservation, risk classification, and compliance record management. By leveraging decentralized identity technologies, ETHOS mitigates risks associated with data centralization and unauthorized access, while simultaneously supporting regulatory audits and compliance. South et al. (South et al., 2025) discuss mechanisms for authenticated delegation among agents. They investigate the sole use of VCs or in combination with OIDC to identify agents and to share verifiable delegations. The LOKA protocol proposed by Ranjan et al. (Ranjan et al., 2025) introduces a framework for ethically governed agent ecosystems. Central to this design is a Universal Agent Identity Layer that leverages DIDs and VCs to establish interoperable and verifiable agent identities. Huang et al. (Huang et al., 2025) propose a zerotrust identity framework built on verifiable agent identities using DIDs and VCs, directly addressing shortcomings of conventional identity and access management systems such as static trust models and limited delegation. Their research highlights how these decentralized mechanisms can create robust, contextsensitive trust and authorization, better suited for dynamic, multi-agent environments. The Agent Network protocol (ANP) also leverages DIDs as a mechanism to uniquely identify agents (Chang et al., 2025). Unlike ledger-based approaches, ANP anchors DIDs in centrally managed web servers, reflecting a pragmatic but less decentralized design choice. The Networked Agents and Decentralized AI (NANDA) index's integration of DIDs and VCs for agents is underpinned by the AgentFacts model, which provides a structured, machine-readable template for representing agent identity and capabilities (Raskar et al., 2025). This approach allows registries and clients to validate agent authenticity, assess reputation, and facilitate dynamic trust evaluation. Other noteworthy contributions include Hossen et al.'s secure communication framework for decentralized agents (Hossen et al., 2025) and Zou et al.'s BlockA2A protocol for secure, verifiable agent-to-agent interoperability (Zou et al., 2025).
In contrast, our approach integrates the VC exchange directly into the A2A protocol. By employing the DIF presentation proof protocol 3 in combination with JSON-LD-encoded VCs on top of A2A, our design extends an existing agent-to-agent interoperability mechanism with built-in trust establishment based on standardized protocols and formats from the domain of decentralized identity management.
3 https://identity.foundation/presentation-exchange/

testCases.input: How must agents implement mutual authentication protocols for rVCs across different security domains?
testCases.actualOutput:
To implement mutual authentication protocols for rich Verifiable Credentials (rVCs) across different security domains, agents must follow a structured process that ensures trust and verification. According to the paper "AI Agents with Decentralized Identifiers and Verifiable Credentials" (arXiv:2511.02841v2), the mutual authentication process involves several key steps:

1. **Ownership Proof**: Each agent must prove ownership of its Decentralized Identifier (DID) and present supporting rVCs to the other party. This is essential for establishing trust before any interaction occurs.

2. **Role of Verifiable Presentations (VPs)**: During the authentication exchange, agents alternate between the roles of a VP holder and a verifier. The holder presents its DID and rVCs in the form of a VP, while the verifier checks the validity of the VP and the trustworthiness of the issuer. This process is crucial for mutual authentication to be established successfully.

3. **Cross-Domain Trust**: Agents from different security domains can only verify rVCs if they recognize the issuer of the presented rVCs and trust it concerning the claims made. This relationship is termed "organizational trust," which is vital for cross-domain dialogues. Agents must present rVCs that contain more comprehensive information than basic Verifiable Credentials (bVCs) to facilitate this verification process.

4. **Use of Protocols**: The authentication relies on established protocols such as the DIF Presentation Exchange protocol for exchanging VPs and the DIF Credential Manifest protocol for issuing VCs. These protocols help standardize the interactions and ensure secure communication between agents across domains.

5. **Intra-Domain and Inter-Domain Processes**: The agents must undergo an intra-domain attestation process to obtain rVCs before they can engage in inter-domain mutual authentication. This involves a designated authority agent within the same security domain issuing the rVCs after verifying the requesting agent's bVCs.

By adhering to these steps, agents can effectively implement mutual authentication protocols for rVCs across different security domains, ensuring secure and trustworthy interactions.

Section: 4 Concept Within our concept, each agent lives in the realm of a security domain and is in control of its own DID and VCs. All agents of a security domain are deployed by a dedicated orchestrator. Each agent's DID is anchored in a jointly operated distributed ledger that spans multiple security domains. The ledger is considered to be commonly governed by participants originating from different security domains. It acts as a cross-domain trust anchor for DID docs. Only the agent in possession of the private key associated with a DID is authorized to update its ledger-anchored DID doc, while all agents of the same or different security domain are only allowed to read it. This design ensures tamper-resistant and cross-domain persistence of an agent's identifier and the associated verification material in the form of public keys. So as per definition, each agent has inherent confidence in the operation of the ledger. For secure handling of the agent DID's private key and the VCs themselves, every agent is equipped with a digital wallet. When initiating a dialogue, agents must mutually authenticate, regardless of whether they belong to the same or different security domains and regardless of the dialogue's purpose, e.g., attestation or service invocation. This zero trust-compliant approach requires each agent to prove ownership of its DID and to present supporting VCs to the other party. The VCs must be cryptographically bound to the DID under investigation. During this exchange, both agents alternate between the roles of a VC holder and a VP verifier: the holder presents its DID and VCs in the form of a VP, while the verifier checks the validity and issuer trustworthiness. If both parties approve the validity of each other's VPs, they are mutually authenticated respectively established trust among each other. At deployment, an agent receives basic (bVCs) or rich VCs (rVCs), depending on its initial role. bVCs encode only minimal information, such as the fact that the entity is an agent, without specifying roles, attributes, capabilities, or authorizations. They are only issued by the security domain's orchestrator. Hence, a bVC contains the orchestrator's DID as the issuer's identifier. While the orchestrator holds its own DID outside the ledger, its DID doc with its verification material is made available to all agents within its security domain. The purpose of bVCs is to empower freshly-deployed agents to trustfully identify themselves to peers of the same security domain in order to receive rVCs. The latter specify additional identity attributes such as roles, capabilities, or authorizations of an agent. Obtaining rVCs after deployment involves an intra-domain attestation process. For this, a freshly-deployed agent approaches a designated authority agent of the same security domain that is in charge to equip agents with rVCs. The attestation is then accomplished through a dialog where one acts as a rVC requester and the other as a rVC issuer. As a dialog requires mutual authentication, the requesting agent presents its bVCs, while the issuer presents its own rVCs. Once both sides are verified, the issuer creates and hands over the desired rVC, which the receiving agent then stores in its wallet for later use. Section: 7 Conclusion and Future Work

This article presented a concept and an experimental setup in which LLM-based AI agents are equipped with self-controlled, ledger-anchored digital identities based on DIDs and VCs. The approach builds on standards originating from the Web3 ecosystem that were originally conceived as technical foundations for selfsovereign digital identities of natural persons. When applied to AI agents, however, these standards enable secure mutual authentication and the establishment of diverse trust relationships across security domains.
The experimental setup employs the DIF presentation proof protocol together with JSON-LD encoded VCs to enable mutual VP exchange. The communication between agents is realized through the framework's native mechanisms in intra-domain scenarios and through the latest A2A protocol in the interdomain scenario. The issuance of VCs is conducted using the DIF Credential Manifest protocol. Despite being applied only in the intra-domain scenario, the attestation of claims can also be conducted across domains, e.g., to issue cross-domain authorizations in the form of VCs. The intra- and inter-domain verifiability of claims becomes possible by anchoring the required key material of the agents' DIDs in a commonly accessible ledger. Agents capable of issuing VCs were introduced to enable future agents to spawn other agents and equip them with verifiable roles, capabilities, and delegations in the form of VCs.
Trust between two agents is established under the assumption that both parties trust the operation of the ledger (technical root of trust) as well as the entities that issued the presented VCs, namely the other domain's issuer (organizational root of trust). But it remains unresolved how trustworthy issuers are identified and designated, and under what legal framework they can be relied upon. The electronic Identification, Authentication and Trust Services (eIDAS) 12 EU regulation has established a legal framework to determine, monitor, and share lists of trusted issuers. Although aimed at natural persons and legal entities, it could be adapted to AI agents acting on their behalf. Future work should therefore not only address tech- nical integration but also explore governance models and policy frameworks that ensure consistent trust management across heterogeneous agent ecosystems.
12 https://eur-lex.europa.eu/eli/reg/2014/910/oj
The experimental setup demonstrates the technical feasibility of the proposed approach but also reveals its limitations once the LLM of an agent is in sole charge to orchestrate security-related procedures. This design decision led to an improvable completion rate for all tested LLMs. It is also the root cause of an increased LLM usage which in turn extends the procedures' duration significantly and results in increased costs. While this design decision helps to gain interesting insights of an LLM as the controller of a security procedure, its practical applicability is at least questionable if only because in one evaluation run both agents agreed to skip the authentication in one direction against the policies stated in the system prompt. However, the evaluation results are strongly dependent on the concrete implementation under study and therefore should not be interpreted as evidence that delegating the orchestration of security procedures to an LLM is fundamentally impractical. As a next step, we plan to migrate the VC/VP routing logic from the LLM to a deterministic component of the agent and let the LLM be in charge to trigger dialogues, to decide whether VCs are shared with other agents based on data protection and privacy policies, and to interpret structured as well as unstructured claims for trust establishing purposes.

testCases.input: How do self-sovereign digital identities and verifiable credentials operate within multi-agent systems for trust establishment?
testCases.actualOutput:
Self-sovereign digital identities (DIDs) and verifiable credentials (VCs) play a crucial role in establishing trust within multi-agent systems, particularly in scenarios where agents interact across organizational boundaries. The framework proposed in "AI Agents with Decentralized Identifiers and Verifiable Credentials" (arXiv:2511.02841v2) outlines how these technologies can facilitate secure and autonomous trust relationships among agents.

Each AI agent is equipped with a self-controlled, ledger-anchored DID, which serves as a unique identifier that verifies ownership through public key material stored on a distributed ledger. This setup allows agents to authenticate themselves at the onset of a dialogue. Alongside DIDs, agents utilize VCs, which are issued by trusted third parties and can contain various claims about the agent's identity, capabilities, and authorizations. These VCs are cryptographically signed, ensuring their integrity and enabling cross-domain verifiability [1].

The process of trust establishment begins with agents presenting their DIDs and associated VCs during interactions. For intra-domain communication, agents can mutually authenticate and exchange VCs, thereby establishing trust based on recognized issuers and their claims. However, challenges arise in inter-domain scenarios where agents may not recognize VCs from other domains due to the absence of issuer documentation. In such cases, agents must rely on "rVCs" (revocable VCs) that extend beyond the limited information of "bVCs" (basic VCs) to ensure trustworthiness [2].

The framework emphasizes that trust is built on two roots: the technical trust in the ledger's operation and the organizational trust in the VC issuers. While the technical feasibility of this approach has been demonstrated, the paper also highlights unresolved issues regarding the identification and designation of trustworthy issuers, suggesting that future work should explore governance models to ensure consistent trust management across diverse agent ecosystems [3].

VCs are explicitly allowed to carry claims in the form of unstructured data such as natural language text, images, or audio. Since modern LLM-based AI agents are able to produce and interpret unstructured content, they can issue and verify unstructured, schemaless claims about other agents. These novel types of claims can bootstrap automated and dynamic trust establishment in multi-agent and cross-domain ecosystems, as different domains do not need to go through an extensive standardization process to reach an agreement on a common rigid VC schema.

AI Agents with Decentralized Identifiers and Verifiable Credentials

Section: 7 Conclusion and Future Work

This article presented a concept and an experimental setup in which LLM-based AI agents are equipped with self-controlled, ledger-anchored digital identities based on DIDs and VCs. The approach builds on standards originating from the Web3 ecosystem that were originally conceived as technical foundations for selfsovereign digital identities of natural persons. When applied to AI agents, however, these standards enable secure mutual authentication and the establishment of diverse trust relationships across security domains.
The experimental setup employs the DIF presentation proof protocol together with JSON-LD encoded VCs to enable mutual VP exchange. The communication between agents is realized through the framework's native mechanisms in intra-domain scenarios and through the latest A2A protocol in the interdomain scenario. The issuance of VCs is conducted using the DIF Credential Manifest protocol. Despite being applied only in the intra-domain scenario, the attestation of claims can also be conducted across domains, e.g., to issue cross-domain authorizations in the form of VCs. The intra- and inter-domain verifiability of claims becomes possible by anchoring the required key material of the agents' DIDs in a commonly accessible ledger. Agents capable of issuing VCs were introduced to enable future agents to spawn other agents and equip them with verifiable roles, capabilities, and delegations in the form of VCs.
Trust between two agents is established under the assumption that both parties trust the operation of the ledger (technical root of trust) as well as the entities that issued the presented VCs, namely the other domain's issuer (organizational root of trust). But it remains unresolved how trustworthy issuers are identified and designated, and under what legal framework they can be relied upon. The electronic Identification, Authentication and Trust Services (eIDAS) 12 EU regulation has established a legal framework to determine, monitor, and share lists of trusted issuers. Although aimed at natural persons and legal entities, it could be adapted to AI agents acting on their behalf. Future work should therefore not only address tech- nical integration but also explore governance models and policy frameworks that ensure consistent trust management across heterogeneous agent ecosystems.
12 https://eur-lex.europa.eu/eli/reg/2014/910/oj
The experimental setup demonstrates the technical feasibility of the proposed approach but also reveals its limitations once the LLM of an agent is in sole charge to orchestrate security-related procedures. This design decision led to an improvable completion rate for all tested LLMs. It is also the root cause of an increased LLM usage which in turn extends the procedures' duration significantly and results in increased costs. While this design decision helps to gain interesting insights of an LLM as the controller of a security procedure, its practical applicability is at least questionable if only because in one evaluation run both agents agreed to skip the authentication in one direction against the policies stated in the system prompt. However, the evaluation results are strongly dependent on the concrete implementation under study and therefore should not be interpreted as evidence that delegating the orchestration of security procedures to an LLM is fundamentally impractical. As a next step, we plan to migrate the VC/VP routing logic from the LLM to a deterministic component of the agent and let the LLM be in charge to trigger dialogues, to decide whether VCs are shared with other agents based on data protection and privacy policies, and to interpret structured as well as unstructured claims for trust establishing purposes.

AI Agents with Decentralized Identifiers and Verifiable Credentials

Section: 3 Related Work

Equipping agents with DIDs and VCs has recently attracted significant attention as a foundation for secure and privacy-preserving identity management in multi- agent ecosystems. Chaffer et al. (Chaffer et al., 2024) present the ETHOS framework, which adopts the SSI paradigm for agents. Their work highlights benefits in terms of privacy preservation, risk classification, and compliance record management. By leveraging decentralized identity technologies, ETHOS mitigates risks associated with data centralization and unauthorized access, while simultaneously supporting regulatory audits and compliance. South et al. (South et al., 2025) discuss mechanisms for authenticated delegation among agents. They investigate the sole use of VCs or in combination with OIDC to identify agents and to share verifiable delegations. The LOKA protocol proposed by Ranjan et al. (Ranjan et al., 2025) introduces a framework for ethically governed agent ecosystems. Central to this design is a Universal Agent Identity Layer that leverages DIDs and VCs to establish interoperable and verifiable agent identities. Huang et al. (Huang et al., 2025) propose a zerotrust identity framework built on verifiable agent identities using DIDs and VCs, directly addressing shortcomings of conventional identity and access management systems such as static trust models and limited delegation. Their research highlights how these decentralized mechanisms can create robust, contextsensitive trust and authorization, better suited for dynamic, multi-agent environments. The Agent Network protocol (ANP) also leverages DIDs as a mechanism to uniquely identify agents (Chang et al., 2025). Unlike ledger-based approaches, ANP anchors DIDs in centrally managed web servers, reflecting a pragmatic but less decentralized design choice. The Networked Agents and Decentralized AI (NANDA) index's integration of DIDs and VCs for agents is underpinned by the AgentFacts model, which provides a structured, machine-readable template for representing agent identity and capabilities (Raskar et al., 2025). This approach allows registries and clients to validate agent authenticity, assess reputation, and facilitate dynamic trust evaluation. Other noteworthy contributions include Hossen et al.'s secure communication framework for decentralized agents (Hossen et al., 2025) and Zou et al.'s BlockA2A protocol for secure, verifiable agent-to-agent interoperability (Zou et al., 2025).
In contrast, our approach integrates the VC exchange directly into the A2A protocol. By employing the DIF presentation proof protocol 3 in combination with JSON-LD-encoded VCs on top of A2A, our design extends an existing agent-to-agent interoperability mechanism with built-in trust establishment based on standardized protocols and formats from the domain of decentralized identity management.
3 https://identity.foundation/presentation-exchange/

AI Agents with Decentralized Identifiers and Verifiable Credentials

Section: 1 INTRODUCTION

The advent of LLM-based AI agents has opened new opportunities for enhancing human productivity and decision-making (Brynjolfsson et al., 2025). A single agent can autonomously retrieve information, perform calculations, automate workflows, and interface with digital services on behalf of its user. Such capabilities already demonstrate tangible benefits in personal assistance and task execution. However, the true potential of agents emerges when they are able to interact and collaborate among each other across organizational boundaries (Sharma et al., 2025). Through agent-to-agent communication, tasks that exceed the scope of an individual agent can be accomplished collaboratively. For instance, while one agent may support a user in planning a vacation by identifying preferences and budget constraints, it is only through secure and trusted interaction with external agents of travel agencies, airlines, and hotels that the full process of planning and booking a holiday can be autonomously and firmly executed.

b https://orcid.org/0009-0007-2192-5968
c https://orcid.org/0000-0002-4356-5613
This shift from isolated single-agent operation to cross-domain multi-agent collaboration comes with new challenges such as interoperability (Sharma et al., 2025), security (Ko et al., 2025) (Kong et al., 2025) (Schroeder de Witt, 2025), and trust (Huang et al., 2025) (Raza et al., 2025). An important step toward addressing interoperability is the recently published Agent2Agent (A2A) protocol 1 , which provides a standardized interaction layer among agents that remains agnostic to the underlying agent frameworks. Enhanced with payment capabilities as introduced by Vaziry et al. (Vaziry et al., 2025) and later implemented by AP2 2 , it may mark the start of agents to become economic actors. In terms of security, A2A builds upon well-established and widely deployed mechanisms from the Web ecosystem, e.g., TLS with x.509 certificates or OpenIDConnect (OIDC).
1 https://a2a-protocol.org
2 https://github.com/google-agentic-commerce/AP2
However, the reliance on traditional web security also carries over its inherent limitations. Web-based access control was originally designed for humancentric use cases, where end-users explicitly initiate sessions, consent to access, and manage credentials. In contrast, agents are expected to operate autonomously and at scale, which exposes shortcomings such as limited support for delegation of authority, insufficient contextualization of trust decisions, and reliance on static trust models that fail to adapt dynamically to a changing context (Huang et al., 2025). These constraints highlight the need for rethinking security and trust frameworks tailored specifically for LLM-based AI agents in multi-agent ecosystems.
In this article, we propose to equip each AI agent with a self-controlled digital identity, comprising a ledger-anchored Decentralized Identifier (DID) (W3C, 2022) and a set of Verifiable Credentials (VCs) (W3C, 2025). A DID is a self-issued identifier whose public key material verifies ownership. The key material can be anchored in a commonly accessible distributed ledger, which serves as the authoritative source of truth for the cryptographic bindings of the DID with its public keys. VCs, in contrast, are issued by third parties and flexibly encode claims about an agent, ranging from basic identity attributes over fine-grained authorizations to complex assertions. A VC is cryptographically signed by an issuer with its DID, making it tamper-resistant and verifiable across domains. Together, ledger-anchored DIDs and offledger VCs empower agents to establish in an autonomous and privacy-preserving manner all kinds of trust relationships among each other, without involving VC issuers. Beyond introducing the concept, we also present a prototypical implementation and its comprehensive evaluation.
The article starts in Section 2 with a brief description of the DID and VCs concepts, focusing on their application to agents. Section 3 discusses latest approaches that make use of DID and/or VCs to equip agents with verifiable identities. Section 4 then introduces the proposed framework in detail while Section 5 describes its prototypical implementation. An experimental setup and its evaluation are investigated in Section 6. Section 7 concludes with a short summary of the findings and sketches the logical next steps towards an implementation suitable for practical use.

AI Agents with Decentralized Identifiers and Verifiable Credentials

Section: 1 INTRODUCTION

The advent of LLM-based AI agents has opened new opportunities for enhancing human productivity and decision-making (Brynjolfsson et al., 2025). A single agent can autonomously retrieve information, perform calculations, automate workflows, and interface with digital services on behalf of its user. Such capabilities already demonstrate tangible benefits in personal assistance and task execution. However, the true potential of agents emerges when they are able to interact and collaborate among each other across organizational boundaries (Sharma et al., 2025). Through agent-to-agent communication, tasks that exceed the scope of an individual agent can be accomplished collaboratively. For instance, while one agent may support a user in planning a vacation by identifying preferences and budget constraints, it is only through secure and trusted interaction with external agents of travel agencies, airlines, and hotels that the full process of planning and booking a holiday can be autonomously and firmly executed.
a https://orcid.org/0000-0001-6921-294X
b https://orcid.org/0009-0007-2192-5968
c https://orcid.org/0000-0002-4356-5613
This shift from isolated single-agent operation to cross-domain multi-agent collaboration comes with new challenges such as interoperability (Sharma et al., 2025), security (Ko et al., 2025) (Kong et al., 2025) (Schroeder de Witt, 2025), and trust (Huang et al., 2025) (Raza et al., 2025). An important step toward addressing interoperability is the recently published Agent2Agent (A2A) protocol 1 , which provides a standardized interaction layer among agents that remains agnostic to the underlying agent frameworks. Enhanced with payment capabilities as introduced by Vaziry et al. (Vaziry et al., 2025) and later implemented by AP2 2 , it may mark the start of agents to become economic actors. In terms of security, A2A builds upon well-established and widely deployed mechanisms from the Web ecosystem, e.g., TLS with x.509 certificates or OpenIDConnect (OIDC).
1 https://a2a-protocol.org
2 https://github.com/google-agentic-commerce/AP2
However, the reliance on traditional web security also carries over its inherent limitations. Web-based access control was originally designed for humancentric use cases, where end-users explicitly initiate sessions, consent to access, and manage credentials. In contrast, agents are expected to operate autonomously and at scale, which exposes shortcomings such as limited support for delegation of authority, insufficient contextualization of trust decisions, and reliance on static trust models that fail to adapt dynamically to a changing context (Huang et al., 2025). These constraints highlight the need for rethinking security and trust frameworks tailored specifically for LLM-based AI agents in multi-agent ecosystems.
In this article, we propose to equip each AI agent with a self-controlled digital identity, comprising a ledger-anchored Decentralized Identifier (DID) (W3C, 2022) and a set of Verifiable Credentials (VCs) (W3C, 2025). A DID is a self-issued identifier whose public key material verifies ownership. The key material can be anchored in a commonly accessible distributed ledger, which serves as the authoritative source of truth for the cryptographic bindings of the DID with its public keys. VCs, in contrast, are issued by third parties and flexibly encode claims about an agent, ranging from basic identity attributes over fine-grained authorizations to complex assertions. A VC is cryptographically signed by an issuer with its DID, making it tamper-resistant and verifiable across domains. Together, ledger-anchored DIDs and offledger VCs empower agents to establish in an autonomous and privacy-preserving manner all kinds of trust relationships among each other, without involving VC issuers. Beyond introducing the concept, we also present a prototypical implementation and its comprehensive evaluation.
The article starts in Section 2 with a brief description of the DID and VCs concepts, focusing on their application to agents. Section 3 discusses latest approaches that make use of DID and/or VCs to equip agents with verifiable identities. Section 4 then introduces the proposed framework in detail while Section 5 describes its prototypical implementation. An experimental setup and its evaluation are investigated in Section 6. Section 7 concludes with a short summary of the findings and sketches the logical next steps towards an implementation suitable for practical use.

testCases.input: What role does the NgramRL system play in enhancing RL post-training via n-gram caching?
testCases.actualOutput:
The NgramRL system plays a crucial role in enhancing reinforcement learning (RL) post-training by utilizing a rollout-aware n-gram caching mechanism. This approach addresses the high computational costs associated with rollout generation during RL post-training, particularly in the context of Group Relative Policy Optimization (GRPO) [1, 2].

NgramRL maintains a per-prompt n-gram cache built from prior rollouts, which allows it to propose draft tokens efficiently. This cache is constructed from the outputs of the policy's previous rollouts, ensuring that the drafts remain aligned with the evolving policy and do not become stale, as would be the case with a fixed drafter [2, 3]. By leveraging the temporal locality of prompts—where rollouts of the same prompt share significant overlaps—NgramRL can accelerate the rollout process without requiring additional model parameters or persistent GPU memory [1, 3].

During each training step, NgramRL queries the n-gram cache for the longest matching sequence from the current context and proposes it as a draft token. The policy then verifies these proposals in a single forward pass, preserving the output distribution and ensuring that the accuracy and convergence of the model remain unchanged [4, 5]. This method not only speeds up the rollout process but also allows for a significant increase in the number of tokens committed per forward pass, achieving up to 1.99 times more than traditional methods like SuffixDecoding [2, 3].

Additionally, NgramRL incorporates an adaptive fan-out prefetcher that prepares drafts for likely verification outcomes, further optimizing the decoding process by minimizing host time and maximizing GPU utilization [2, 5]. Overall, NgramRL effectively transforms the redundancy in prompt rollouts into a powerful tool for accelerating RL post-training while maintaining high fidelity in output generation.

The design rests on one property of RL post-training. GRPO [20] revisits the same prompts across steps and epochs, and the policy changes only incrementally between them, so a prompt's completions repeat those it produced earlier in training. Figure 2 illustrates this phenomenon: rollouts of the same Spider [23] (text-to-SQL) prompt one epoch apart share only the query skeleton early on and become verbatim identical by late training. NgramRL turns this redundancy into accepted drafts, a signal a single-generation drafter cannot utilize.

testCases.input: How does NgramRL's adaptive n-gram caching compare to traditional methods in optimizing RL post-training?
testCases.actualOutput:
NgramRL introduces a novel approach to optimizing reinforcement learning (RL) post-training through its adaptive n-gram caching mechanism, which significantly differs from traditional methods. Traditional speculative decoding methods often rely on fixed drafters that require additional trainable parameters and do not adapt to the evolving nature of the RL policy. For instance, methods like SuffixDecoding utilize static caches that do not co-evolve with the policy, leading to lower acceptance rates during generation [1, 5].

In contrast, NgramRL builds a self-updating, per-prompt n-gram cache from recent policy rollouts. This cache is specifically designed to leverage the temporal locality of prompts, meaning that it can effectively reuse high-quality drafts from previous rollouts as the policy incrementally updates. The authors note that "across consecutive epochs, a prior rollout covers 48-96% of a later rollout," indicating a high degree of overlap that NgramRL capitalizes on [1, 2]. This dynamic caching mechanism allows NgramRL to maintain alignment with the policy, avoiding the pitfalls of stale or mismatched drafts that traditional methods face.

Moreover, NgramRL employs an adaptive fan-out prefetcher that prepares drafts for likely verification outcomes, which helps to hide CPU time and optimize GPU utilization. This results in a significant performance boost, achieving "up to 1.99× more tokens per forward than SuffixDecoding" and "7.0× more than prompt-lookup decoding" [1, 4]. The integration of this adaptive caching strategy not only enhances efficiency but also preserves the output distribution, making NgramRL a more effective solution for structured generation tasks in RL post-training compared to traditional methods.

Section: 1 Introduction

Reinforcement learning post-training [17, 19], and Group Relative Policy Optimization (GRPO) in particular [20], has become central to improving LLM reasoning [6]. But it is expensive, and the cost is dominated by the rollout generation. Each GRPO step autoregressively samples many completions per prompt before any gradient is To this end, we propose NgramRL, a rollout-aware per-prompt n-gram cache that acts as a model-free drafter for speculative decoding during RL post-training. For each prompt, NgramRL maintains an n-gram table built from that prompt's prior rollouts and proposes continuations by lookup, which the policy verifies. The cache lives in host memory and is queried on the CPU, overlapping GPU computation so that drafting adds no persistent GPU memory and negligible GPU time, and because it is populated by the policy's own outputs it stays aligned with the policy rather than going stale like a fixed drafter. To keep this CPU work off the critical path, NgramRL pairs the cache with an asynchronous multipath prefetch runtime that prefetches the next step's drafts during verification, so the decode iteration collapses to GPU busy time.

We identify and characterize prompt-conditioned temporal locality in RL rollouts. GRPO repeatedly samples the same prompts while updating the policy incrementally, previous rollouts provide high-quality drafts for future epochs. Across consecutive epochs, a prior rollout covers 48-96% of a later rollout, with recurring spans of 7-23 tokens.
We propose NgramRL, a self-updating, per-prompt 𝑛 -gram drafter constructed entirely from recent policy rollouts. Section: 3.1 Overview

As shown in Figure 1, NgramRL is a co-design of a model-free drafter with the RL rollout engine. It accelerates rollout without

The design rests on one property of RL post-training. GRPO [20] revisits the same prompts across steps and epochs, and the policy changes only incrementally between them, so a prompt's completions repeat those it produced earlier in training. Figure 2 illustrates this phenomenon: rollouts of the same Spider [23] (text-to-SQL) prompt one epoch apart share only the query skeleton early on and become verbatim identical by late training. NgramRL turns this redundancy into accepted drafts, a signal a single-generation drafter cannot utilize.
Each prompt owns an 𝑛 -gram cache built from its prior rollouts. During rollout the cache proposes continuations by lookup and the policy verifies them exactly, preserving the output distribution. The cache lives in host memory and is queried on the CPU, so drafting adds no persistent GPU memory and overlaps GPU compute. Section: 3.5 Integration and Generality

We integrate NgramRL into verl's [21] vLLM rollout worker. Adding no parameters and no training, it composes with existing rollout-efficiency methods and applies to any RL-style setup where prompts recur.

NgramRL: Accelerating RL Post-Training for Structured Generation via Rollout-Aware N-gram Speculative Decoding

Section: 5 Conclusion

We presented NgramRL, a rollout-aware speculative-decoding system that exploits prompt-conditioned temporal locality in RL posttraining. NgramRL builds bounded per-prompt 𝑛 -gram caches from recent policy rollouts, yielding self-updating drafts without an auxiliary model, drafter training, or GPU-resident drafter state. An adaptive fan-out prefetcher with a causal budget allocator keeps the host-resident cache off the decode critical path by preparing drafts for likely verification outcomes ( 𝑗, 𝑏 ) , while uncovered requests fall back to sequential lookup without altering the rollout distribution. Across two model families and three workloads, NgramRL commits 3.60-7.77 tokens per target-model forward, up to 1 . 99 × more than SuffixDecoding and 7 . 0 × more than prompt-lookup decoding, and the prefetcher delivers up to 1 . 38 × measured rollout speedup over synchronous execution. These results show that recent same-prompt rollouts are an effective draft source and that outcome-aware CPU-GPU prefetching converts this temporal locality into measured acceleration while preserving exact target sampling.

Section: Acknowledgments

This work was funded in part by NSF (awards #1826967, #1911095, #2003279, #2052809, #2100237, #2112167, and #2112665), and by PRISM and CoCoSys, centers in JUMP 2.0, an SRC program sponsored by DARPA.

NgramRL: Accelerating RL Post-Training for Structured Generation via Rollout-Aware N-gram Speculative Decoding

Section: 2.2 Related Work

Model-based speculative decoding. Speculative decoding [3, 10] pairs a fast drafter with the target, which verifies drafted tokens in parallel while preserving the target's output distribution. Strong methods train the drafter as a separate draft model, additional decoding heads such as Medusa [2], or feature-level draft models such as EAGLE [12]. The crucial difference between this literature and our work is that these drafters add trainable parameters and assume a fixed target. In RL post-training both assumptions fail, since the parameters consume scarce GPU memory and a fixed drafter cannot track a policy that changes every step.
Model-free drafters. A separate line copies previously seen tokens rather than predicting them. Prompt-lookup decoding [18] matches 𝑛 -grams against the current prompt, REST [7] retrieves continuations from a fixed datastore, and Token Recycling [14] reuses candidates discarded during a single decode. These add no parameters, but their evidence is limited to a single generation or a static corpus, so acceptance is low on the free-form traces that RL produces. The closest work is SuffixDecoding [16], which caches token sequences from prior outputs in CPU-side suffix trees and performs best on structured tasks such as text-to-SQL. The crucial difference is the setting. SuffixDecoding serves a fixed model, and its repetition arises from agentic inference pipelines. We operate inside RL training, where the policy is non-stationary and the repetition arises from GRPO revisiting the same prompts. Our per-prompt cache consequently co-evolves with the policy, and acceptance strengthens as training proceeds, a behavior the fixed-target setting does not exhibit.
Structured generation. The highest-value targets for RL posttraining, including text-to-SQL, code generation, and tool and API calls, produce outputs with strong syntactic regularity. Completions of the same prompt share schema tokens, keywords, and boilerplate, so identical tokens recur, and copy-based drafting is known to favor such low-entropy outputs [16]. We show that this regularity is amplified in RL training, where the same prompts are sampled repeatedly, so structured tasks benefit most from rollout-derived 𝑛 -gram caching.
