testCases.name: test_case_31
testCases.input: What specific attributes of the fine-tuned DistilBERT encoder enhance its predictive accuracy on the 9,567-ticket test set compared to non-LLM models?
testCases.actualOutput:
The fine-tuned DistilBERT encoder demonstrates enhanced predictive accuracy on the 9,567-ticket test set due to several specific attributes. Firstly, it achieves the highest accuracy among the non-LLM baselines, with an accuracy of 0.877 and a macro-F1 score of 0.874 after just two epochs of training on a single GPU. This performance is attributed to its ability to learn from a substantial dataset of 33,486 labeled tickets, which allows it to effectively understand the underlying taxonomy of the ticket classification task [1].

In contrast, the prompted LLMs, such as Claude Haiku 4.5 and GPT-4o-mini, while benefiting from few-shot prompting, do not have the same depth of training data. They rely on a limited number of examples (at most 24) and label names without detailed category definitions, which restricts their learning capability compared to DistilBERT [1]. The results indicate that the gap in performance is not merely due to different test examples, as the accuracy of DistilBERT on a common 1,000-ticket subset is 0.879, significantly higher than the best LLM's score of 0.477 on the same tickets [2].

Additionally, the architecture of DistilBERT, being a distilled version of BERT, allows it to maintain a balance between model size and performance, making it efficient for the classification task. The fine-tuning process on tokenized ticket text further optimizes its ability to classify tickets accurately, leveraging its transformer-based architecture to capture contextual information effectively [3]. 

Overall, the combination of extensive training data, effective fine-tuning, and the inherent strengths of the DistilBERT architecture contribute to its superior predictive accuracy compared to non-LLM models.
testCases.expectedOutput: The fine-tuned DistilBERT encoder enhances predictive accuracy on the 9,567-ticket test set through its ability to learn complex patterns and relationships in the data from a large labeled training set (33,486 tickets). It achieves an accuracy of 0.877 and a macro-F1 score of 0.874 after just two epochs of training, outperforming non-LLM models like the sigmoid-calibrated linear SVM and TF-IDF-based classifiers. This superior performance is attributed to its deep learning architecture, which captures contextual information more effectively than traditional models that rely on simpler feature extraction methods.
retrievalContext:
Cost-Aware Abstention for LLM-Based IT Ticket Classification

Section: A. Base-classifier predictive performance

We compare four non-LLM baselines against eight prompted hosted LLM configurations (Table III). Among nonLLM baselines the fine-tuned encoder is strongest. DistilBERT reaches accuracy 0.877 and macro-F1 0.874 on the full 9,567ticket test set after two epochs of training on a single GPU with batch size 32 and maximum sequence length 256. The next non-LLM baseline is a sigmoid-calibrated linear SVM over TF-IDF features (accuracy 0.863 , macro-F1 0.864 ), followed by the TF-IDF + logistic regression baseline (0.847 / 0.842) and a TF-IDF random forest (0.818 / 0.806).
The best prompted LLM is Claude Haiku 4.5 with k =3 few-shot prompting at 0 . 477 / 0 . 459 . GPT-4o-mini few-shot follows (0.459 / 0.450), then Qwen2.5-7B-Instruct few-shot (0.447 / 0.454) and Llama-3-8B-Instruct-Lite zero-shot (0.378 / 0.284). On the common 1,000-ticket subset, DistilBERT reaches 0.879 and Haiku few-shot 0.477, so the measured gap is not caused by different test examples. It is not, however, a pure capability comparison: the trained models learn the taxonomy from 33,486 labeled tickets, whereas the prompted LLMs receive label names and, at most, 24 examples without category definitions. Ambiguous labels such as Miscellaneous , Internal Project , and Administrative rights make that distinction material. We therefore scope the result to these training and prompt-information regimes.
Few-shot prompting helps three of the four LLMs but hurts Llama-3-8B-Instruct-Lite by 12.3 percentage points. Inspection of the raw outputs shows that the model often emits a conversational preamble ( 'I'll classify the ticket and return the JSON.' ) that uses up the output budget before any JSON
Fig. 2. Class distribution of the 47,837-ticket corpus across the eight categories.
is emitted, which produces a 15.1 % parse-error rate. 2 We dig into this in §V-D.

Cost-Aware Abstention for LLM-Based IT Ticket Classification

Section: B. Test subsample for LLM predictors

Per-call API budget makes evaluating all four LLMs on the full 9,567-ticket test set impractical. The 8 LLM configurations alone issue 8 , 000 test queries on the subsample described below, and scaling to the full test set would multiply that by an order of magnitude. LLMs are therefore evaluated on a stratified 1,000-ticket subsample (seed 42). To assess whether that subset preserves the non-LLM baseline ordering, we re-evaluate every non-LLM baseline on the same 1,000ticket subsample (Table II). Subsample and full-test numbers differ by at most 1.6 percentage points for every baseline. The strongest non-LLM baseline (DistilBERT) reaches 0.879 accuracy on the subsample, versus 0.477 for the best LLM on the same tickets, confirming the same ordering on identical examples.

Section: C. Reproducibility

Runs save configuration, seeds, dataset and split hashes, package versions, and per-ticket outputs. Intervals use 1,000 paired resamples with seed 1337; reported percentage reductions recompute the ratio inside each resample. The public project repository is https://github. com/sachinkg12/RouteGuard; the frozen camera-ready claim manifest, automated recomputation receipt from a separate verification script, tables, text-free per-ticket vectors, and code snapshot are archived as a versioned series at doi:10.5281/zenodo.22609128. The supplement pins the verified x86-64/Python 3.14 environment because estimator refits can vary slightly across architectures; the frozen prediction vectors remain the audit record.

Cost-Aware Abstention for LLM-Based IT Ticket Classification

Section: B. Predictors

We evaluate four non-LLM baselines and four prompted LLMs.
Non-LLM baselines. TF-IDF (term frequency-inverse document frequency) uni- and bi-gram features feed three classifiers. Logistic regression and linear support vector machine (SVM) cap the vocabulary at 100,000 features; random forest caps it at 50,000. The headline baseline is multiclass logistic regression (LR; L2 regularization, C =1 . 0 ). The linear SVM head is a one-vs-rest linear support vector classifier (SVC) wrapped in sigmoid-calibrated probability outputs. The random forest head uses 300 trees with default depth. Separately, the fourth baseline fine-tunes DistilBERT ( distilbert-base-uncased ) on tokenized ticket text from the full training split for two epochs with batch size 32 and maximum sequence length 256. All four are fit on the same train split.
LLM predictors. Each LLM is queried per ticket with a structured prompt (template v1 ; the strict v2 is used only in §V-D) that lists the allowed labels, the ticket text, and an instruction to return JSON {"label": ..., "confidence": ...} . Fewshot variants prepend k =3 exemplars per class (24 in total, class-balanced across the eight categories), drawn only from the training split. The main prompts contain label names and examples but no natural-language category definitions; the comparison therefore characterizes these prompting conditions, not each LLM's intrinsic capability. We use temperature 0 and max_tokens =64 for all main runs. Out-of-set labels are tagged as invalid; malformed JSON is tagged as a parse error. Both invalid labels and parse errors are scored as incorrect predictions and assigned confidence 0; the threshold policies defer such rows rather than auto-route them, while always_route , by definition, routes them and incurs c wrong . The four models are GPT-4o-mini [24], Claude Haiku 4.5 [25], Qwen2.5-7B-Instruct [26], and Llama-3-8BInstruct-Lite [27]. GPT-4o-mini and Claude Haiku are queried through their vendor APIs. 1 The open-weights models use Together AI endpoints Qwen2.5-7B-Instruct-Turbo
1 For reproducibility, the proprietary endpoints and query date were: OpenAI gpt-4o-mini and Anthropic claude-haiku-4-5-20251001 , both queried on 2026-05-22. The Anthropic model is a dated snapshot; the OpenAI alias resolves to the provider's then-current gpt-4o-mini snapshot, so those results reflect the endpoint state on that date.
and Meta-Llama-3-8B-Instruct-Lite , providerdocumented at query time as 8-bit floating point (FP8) and 4-bit integer (INT4), respectively; precision is absent from our saved responses and is not independently verified. We re-run the model families through DeepInfra (provider-documented bfloat16, or BF16) as a cross-provider check that does not isolate quantization; our conclusions are unchanged (§V-E).

Cost-Aware Abstention for LLM-Based IT Ticket Classification

Section: B. Is the confidence signal useful?

Every prompted LLM is overconfident: raw ECE spans [0 . 332 , 0 . 594] , and GPT-4o-mini few-shot assigns confidence 1.000 to every ticket despite 0.459 accuracy. Isotonic regression fitted on the disjoint calibration subset reduces LLM ECE to [0 . 014 , 0 . 049] , an 86-98 % relative reduction.
That ECE result must not be read as improved error ranking. Isotonic is monotone and changes correctness AUROC by at most 0.007 in these runs; AURC also does not improve consistently (Table III). The limiting example is GPT-4o-mini few-shot: raw confidence is the constant 1.000, isotonic maps it to the constant 0.480, and both correctness AUROC and AURC remain 0.500 and 0.541. Isotonic corrects the probability level by mapping a non-discriminative score to the base accuracy; it does not create information that was absent from the score.
Agreement can carry ranking signal, but the voter pool matters. Table IV separates the mixed M =9 pool from the LLMonly M =8 control. The M =8 correctness AUROC spans 0.590-0.773, descriptive evidence that peer-only agreement contains ranking signal on these data. Its ECE also improves over raw confidence in all eight conditions, but ECE alone would not establish discrimination. The mixed pool is better in every listed ECE and AUROC cell, but it includes the supervised TF-IDF + LR vote. Thus M =9 uses no held-out calibration labels when a score is computed, yet it is not free of supervised information. It also requires all predictors at inference.

Cost-Aware Abstention for LLM-Based IT Ticket Classification

Section: C. Confidence and rejection scores

We evaluate probability estimates and ranking signals separately.
Model-reported. For a non-LLM baseline this is the maximum class-probability estimate returned by that model: multinomial probabilities for logistic regression, sigmoid-calibrated outputs for the SVM, tree-vote fractions for the random forest, and softmax for DistilBERT. For LLMs it is the confidence field parsed from the JSON output.
Cross-predictor agreement. Given M predictors evaluated on the same ticket, the agreement-confidence for the primary predictor is the fraction of the M predictors that emit the same label. No held-out labels are used to compute this score at application time. In our mixed configuration M =9 : the four LLMs in zero-shot and few-shot settings (eight prompted variants) plus the classical TF-IDF + LR baseline. Because this pool mixes the eight LLM variants with the stronger classical baseline, an LLM's agreement partly reflects concordance with a more accurate supervised predictor, not peer consensus alone. We therefore also report an LLM-only M =8 control. Operational trade-off: agreement requires running all M predictors at inference. Because the pool is heterogeneous, its dollar cost and latency depend on the endpoints and are not necessarily M × those of the primary alone. Isotonic incurs one calibration-time pass per prompted predictor and a constant-time lookup at inference.
Isotonic regression on a held-out calibration split. LLMemitted confidence fi elds are bounded in [0 , 1] but are not logits, so parametric Platt or temperature scaling do not apply cleanly. We instead fit one isotonic regression per prompted LLM condition on the calibration split: pairs { ( c i , 1 [ˆ y i = y i ]) } of raw confidence and ground-truth correctness, mapped via sklearn.isotonic.IsotonicRegression [28] (monotone non-decreasing, output clipped to [0 , 1] ) into a recalibration c ↦→ ˆ Pr( correct ) . For each LLM predictor we fit on a stratified 500-ticket subsample of the calibration split (4,000 calibration queries across the 8 prompted variants). Calibration and test splits are disjoint : the isotonic mapping is learned only from calibration pairs and applied unchanged to test confidences. ECE is computed with 10 equal-width bins on test predictions.
Discrimination metrics. ECE measures probability-level calibration but not whether confidence ranks correct predictions above errors. We therefore report correctness AUROC (ties receive half credit) and area under the risk-coverage curve (AURC; lower is better). Since LLM scores contain many ties, our AURC adds each equal-score group as a block and integrates the right-continuous risk step, avoiding arbitrary ordering within ties.
Nontrivial rejection comparators. For TF-IDF + LR we also use the top-two probability margin p (1) -p (2) and normalized inverse entropy 1 -H ( p ) / log K . Each score's threshold is selected on calibration over a 0.01-spaced grid in [0 , 1] and then evaluated once on test.

testCases.input: What is PR-Issue misalignment in SWE-bench benchmarks, and what are its implications?
testCases.actualOutput:
PR-Issue misalignment in SWE-bench benchmarks refers to discrepancies between a pull request (PR) and the issue description it is linked to. This misalignment can occur when a PR does not exclusively and completely address the stated problem in the issue, leading to potential evaluation fairness and reliability issues. For instance, a PR might bundle fixes for multiple issues, introduce new defects, or rely on information clarified in later discussions rather than the original issue description. Such misalignments can result in benchmarks that do not accurately reflect the capabilities of models being evaluated, as they may learn from incomplete or unrelated patches rather than fixes that are faithful to the stated issues [3].

In a study of SWE-bench Verified, it was found that 13.6% of instances exhibited PR-Issue misalignment, with the most prevalent patterns being defective PRs (44.1%), PR scope creep (32.4%), and incomplete specifications (26.5%) [4]. The implications of this misalignment are significant: it can lead to misleading evaluation results, as misaligned instances are harder for models to resolve. For example, among instances that were never resolved by any of the 131 leaderboard agents, 41.2% were found to be misaligned, suggesting that these instances introduce extraneous difficulty that complicates evaluation beyond mere task complexity [5]. Furthermore, excluding misaligned instances from evaluation can lead to substantial changes in agent rankings, indicating that reliance on such instances can distort performance assessments [2]. 

Overall, PR-Issue misalignment highlights the need for careful construction and validation of benchmarks to ensure that they provide reliable and fair evaluations of automated issue-solving capabilities in software engineering [1].

In a systematic study, it was found that 13.6% of instances in SWE-bench Verified exhibited such misalignment. The implications are significant: misalignment can lead to increased difficulty in resolving issues, as evidenced by the finding that 41.2% of instances unresolved by agents were misaligned. This highlights the need for automated detection and categorization of PR-Issue misalignment to improve resolution rates and ensure accurate assessments of agent performance.

Section: 2.1 Study Design

2.1.1 Dataset. We conduct our study on SWE-bench Verified [23], a human-validated subset of 500 SWE-Bench [29] instances. We select it for two reasons: (1) its human validation represents a high-quality baseline, so misalignments found here likely reflect broader issues in other SWE-bench-like benchmarks; (2) its official experiments repository [2] provides per-instance resolution data for 131 leaderboard agents, enabling quantitative analysis for RQ2.
2.1.2 Method. Manual Examination Process. Following established practices in qualitative SE research [18, 24], we apply open coding [36] to derive a misalignment taxonomy (RQ1). First, we collect per instance: issue-side artifacts (description, discussion), PR-side artifacts (description, discussion, code review, commits, changed files), and cross-reference metadata. Then, we code all 500 instances, iteratively grouping codes into higher-level categories to form a draft taxonomy; a single instance may exhibit multiple patterns. Last, the draft taxonomy was reviewed by the second author; disagreements were resolved with a third author until consensus.
Leaderboard Data Collection. To assess the impact of misalignment on evaluation reliability, we collect per-instance resolution data from the official SWE-bench experiments repository [2], recording per-instance resolution counts for 131 leaderboard agents.

PAIChecker: Uncovering and Checking PR-Issue Misalignment in SWE-Bench-Like Benchmarks

Section: 4.1 Evaluation Dataset

We evaluate on two datasets disjoint from our preliminary study: SWE-Gym[32](2,438 Python tasks) and SWE-bench Multilingual [29] (300 tasks covering C, C++, Go, Java, JavaScript/TypeScript, PHP, Ruby, and Rust). Selection followed five criteria: (i) SWE-bench-style automated PR-Issue pairing; (ii) no manual specification rewriting, so raw defects remain observable; (iii) feasible for full manual annotation yet sufficiently large; (iv) multi-repo and widely adopted; and (v) PR identifiers available for full-content access. Two annotators with development experience independently labeled all instances following our taxonomy (Section 2.2.1), guided by structured questions adapted from SWE-bench annotation instructions [1]. They achieved Cohen's Kappa [33] of 𝜅 = 0 . 91 on binary judgment and 𝜅 = 0 . 86 on fine-grained labeling; disagreements were resolved by a third author. Table 2 summarizes the dataset statistics.
Misalignment rates differ across datasets: 13.6% in SWE-bench Verified (Table 1), 44.3% in SWE-Gym, and 24.3% in SWE-bench Multilingual, largely reflecting SWE-bench Verified's human curation. Patterns tied to underspecification and test coverage drop most sharply in Verified: UL decreases from 15.9% (SWE-Gym) and 3.0% (Multilingual) to 0.2%, IS from 14.0% and 4.3% to 3.6%, and SC from 17.6% and 11.0% to 4.4%. In contrast, deeper PR-Issue relationship defects remain comparable: DP stays near 6.0-8.0%, and FP remains low across all three datasets (0.6%, 4.5%, 0.7%). These defects are harder to infer from the task alone and thus more likely to escape human curation.

PAIChecker: Uncovering and Checking PR-Issue Misalignment in SWE-Bench-Like Benchmarks

Section: 1 Introduction The emergence of large language models (LLMs) capable of code generation and program repair has spurred the need for rigorous, real-world benchmarks [25, 27-29, 46]. Among them, SWEbench [29] has become one of the most influential benchmarks for evaluating LLMs on automated issue solving tasks [38, 44, 47, 49, 54]. SWE-bench constructs task instances from real-world GitHub repositories, using issue descriptions as problem statements and the corresponding pull request (PR) patches as test oracles. Following its success, several SWE-bench-like benchmarks have emerged to ∗ Junjielong Xu and Pinjia He are the corresponding authors. This work is licensed under a Creative Commons Attribution 4.0 International License. ASE '26, Munich, Germany © 2026 Copyright held by the owner/author(s). ACM ISBN 979-8-4007-2882-2/2026/10 https://doi.org/10.1145/3832783.3837557 Junjielong Xu ∗ The Chinese University of Hong Kong, Shenzhen China junjielongxu@link.cuhk.edu.cn Pinjia He ∗ The Chinese University of Hong Kong, Shenzhen China hepinjia@cuhk.edu.cn address various limitations, a non-exhaustive list includes SWEbench Verified [23], SWE-Gym [32], SWE-PolyBench [35], SWESmith [48], and SWE-Bench-Live [52]. These benchmarks largely adopt the same construction pipeline: they filter PRs by quality criteria, then use regular expressions to extract linked issues from PR descriptions, forming PR-Issue pairs as task instances. However, this construction pipeline rests on a critical assumption: that each PR is well-aligned with its linked issue, i.e., the PR exclusively and completely addresses the stated problem, and the issue fully specifies what the PR solves. In practice, this assumption is frequently violated. A PR may bundle fixes for multiple issues, serve as a follow-up to a previous incomplete fix, introduce new defects alongside the intended fix, or implement details clarified only in later discussions rather than the original description. Such misalignment renders the benchmark instance problematic: the problem statement may not fully describe the expected solution, or the test oracle may evaluate aspects unrelated to the stated problem , directly undermining evaluation fairness and reliability. Beyond evaluation, the same construction pipeline also underlies trainingoriented datasets for code LLMs and software agents. Misaligned PR-Issue pairs therefore become noisy supervision, encouraging models to learn incomplete, unrelated, or even defective patches rather than fixes faithful to the stated issue. In this paper, we present a systematic study of PR-Issue misalignment in SWE-bench-like benchmarks, where PR-Issue misalignment refers to discrepancies between a pull request code implementation and the issue description it is linked to in the dataset. We manually analyze all 500 instances in SWE-bench Verified [23] and find that 13.6% exhibit misalignment. We further classify these misalignments into five patterns spanning 11 fine-grained scenarios. To quantify the impact of misalignment, we correlate it with agent resolution rates and find that 41.2% of instances never resolved by any of the 131 leaderboard agents are misaligned. These findings motivate the need for automated detection and categorization of PR-Issue misalignment at scale. However, detecting misalignment directly from the code implementation and issue description is challenging, as the intent reflected in code is inherently ambiguous. This ambiguity arises from the nature of code changes: in complex cases, the intended behavior may depend on modifications spanning hundreds or thousands of lines, while in simpler cases, the implemented behavior may still be incomplete or defective. By contrast, PR-side textual artifacts, such as PR descriptions and discussions, often summarize changes at a level of abstraction similar to issues [8-10], and their shared natural-language form makes the comparison between them far more straightforward and reliable. This asymmetry between textual artifacts and code motivates the key design principle of our approach, namely the text-driven, code-validation principle, which first assesses alignment based on textual evidence and then validates it against code. We assess impact in two ways: correlating misalignment labels with perinstance resolution counts across 131 leaderboard agents, and recomputing the leaderboard [3] after excluding misaligned instances. Misalignment-Resolution Correlation. (1) Methodology. We bucket the 500 instances by the number of resolving agents and compute each bucket's misalignment rate (Figure 2). (2) Results and Discussion. Among the 500 instances, 34 have never been resolved by any of the 131 leaderboard agents. Of these, 14 (41.2%) exhibit PR-Issue misalignment, suggesting that the hardest instances may correlate with agents due to unstated evaluation requirements, not task complexity alone. More broadly, Figure 2 shows a monotonic decrease in misalignment rate as instances are resolved by more agents: from 41.2% among never-resolved instances to 5.7% for those resolved by over 100 agents. Well-aligned instances are solvable by many agents, whereas misaligned instances introduce extraneous difficulty that few agents overcome by coincidence. testCases.input: Elucidate the multi-agent architecture of PaiChecker in detecting nuanced PR-Issue misalignment scenarios.
testCases.actualOutput:
PaiChecker employs a sophisticated multi-agent architecture designed to detect and categorize nuanced PR-Issue misalignment scenarios through a structured three-phase process.

**Phase I: Specific Misalignment Identification** involves three specialized subagents, each focusing on distinct misalignment patterns. The **Issue Analyzer** targets Incomplete Specification (IS) by comparing issue descriptions with their discussion threads to identify any missing components or redefinitions. The **PR Scope Analyzer** detects PR Scope Creep (SC) and Unspecified Literals (UL) by establishing a baseline from the issue's requested scope and checking if the PR exceeds it. Lastly, the **PR Connection Analyzer** identifies Defective PR (DP) and Follow-up PR (FP) by analyzing temporal relationships between the current PR and related PRs, utilizing GitHub API access to retrieve relevant data [1, 3].

**Phase II: Labels Synthesis** synthesizes the outputs from the three subagents into preliminary labels. This phase acts as a coordinator that aggregates evidence, allowing for the identification of misalignments that may not fit predefined patterns. It also includes a self-correction mechanism to verify the labels against textual evidence [1, 4].

**Phase III: Code Validation** employs a code validator agent that cross-references the preliminary labels against the actual code implementation. This phase is crucial for filtering out false positives that may arise from textual reasoning alone. The validator can only remove labels, ensuring that the detection process is rigorous and grounded in code-level evidence [2, 4].

Overall, PaiChecker's architecture is designed to leverage specialized reasoning and a text-driven, code-validation principle, enhancing its effectiveness in identifying and categorizing PR-Issue misalignments in software engineering benchmarks [1, 5].

Section: 3.3 Phase III: Code Validation

In this subsection, we describe Phase III, which deploys a code validator agent responsible for code-level self-correction. The preceding phases make detection decisions from textual evidence; the code validator cross-references these decisions against the actual implementation to filter false positives that textual reasoning alone cannot catch. Section: 3.1 Phase I: Specific Misalignment Identification

In this subsection, we describe Phase I, which detects the five misalignment patterns using three parallel subagents, each focused on distinct reasoning: the Issue Analyzer targets Incomplete Specification (IS), primarily drawing on issue-side artifacts; the PR Scope Analyzer targets PR Scope Creep (SC) and Unspecified Literal (UL) through issue-versus-PR scope comparison; and the PR Connection Analyzer targets Defective PR (DP) and Follow-up PR (FP) through temporal cross-PR reasoning. This grouping keeps each subagent's context compact and reasoning focused. All three produce a uniform structured output: (i) a judgment per target pattern, (ii) supporting evidence for text-level self-correction, and (iii) suspicious clues -anomalies outside the subagent's target patterns that support beyond-taxonomy generalization.
3.1.1 Issue Analyzer. The Issue Analyzer operationalizes IS detection by comparing the issue description against its discussion thread. As mentioned in Section 2.2.1: a well-formed bug report comprises three key components: reproduction code, actual behavior, and expected behavior. Based on this, the subagent performs two checks.
First, whether the issue is incomplete: it identifies whether a maintainer explicitly requests the reporter to supplement any of these components, grounding the judgment in community consensus rather than subjective assessment. Second, whether the issue has been redefined: it checks whether any of these components differs between the original description and the discussion; a change in any component signals that the addressed problem has shifted.
3.1.2 PR Scope Analyzer. The PR Scope Analyzer detects SC and UL in a unified pass. Both patterns require establishing the issue's requested scope as a baseline and checking whether the PR exceeds it, so a single subagent establishes the baseline once and verifies both patterns together. This subagent receives the issue description as scope baseline, PR-side text for what the PR claims to deliver, and both patches for UL detection.
Following the text-driven, code-validation principle, SC is triggered only when PR-side textual artifacts explicitly claim work beyond the issue's scope. UL is triggered when all three conditions hold: (1) the test patch asserts a hardcoded literal ( e.g. a string, number, or exception message); (2) the literal is newly added in the code patch as a fixed constant, rather than read from existing metadata; and (3) it does not appear verbatim in the issue description.
3.1.3 PR Connection Analyzer. The PR Connection Analyzer detects DP and FP, both involve temporal relationships between the current PR and other PRs for the same issue. Tracing such crossPR dependency chains requires information beyond the current instance's artifacts, so we equip this subagent with GitHub API access to actively search for and retrieve related PRs.

By contrast, PR-side textual artifacts, such as PR descriptions and discussions, often summarize changes at a level of abstraction similar to issues [8-10], and their shared natural-language form makes the comparison between them far more straightforward and reliable. This asymmetry between textual artifacts and code motivates the key design principle of our approach, namely the text-driven, code-validation principle, which first assesses alignment based on textual evidence and then validates it against code. ASE '26, October 12-16, 2026, Munich, Germany Manyi Wang, Junjielong Xu, and Pinjia He According to this principle, the task is well suited to LLM reasoning and tool-augmented agents, because it is fundamentally a semantic comparison task. We therefore adapt Mini-SWE-Agent [47], augmenting it with task-specific prompts and GitHub API access, as a representative general-purpose agent baseline. However, this approach has three limitations: (1) it lacks specialization: different misalignment patterns require different inputs and reasoning workflows, but a single prompt conflates these heterogeneous requirements and often misses subtle yet critical evidence. (2) it has limited generalizability: when no predefined pattern applies, it tends to force-fit the instance into the nearest known category, even though real-world misalignments often fall outside the taxonomy. (3) it lacks verification mechanism: its predicted label may not match its own textual reasoning as well as the code implementation. We illustrate these limitations in detail in Section 2.3. To address these limitations, we propose PaiChecker ( P RI ssue A lignment Checker), a three-phase multi-agent framework guided by a text-driven, code-validation principle. The first two phases focus on textual analysis, and the third performs code-level verification. Specifically, Phase I addresses limitation(1) through three specialized subagents, each with a focused artifact subset and tailored workflow. Phase II addresses limitation(2) via a coordinator that synthesizes cross-subagent evidence to identify misalignment beyond known patterns. For limitation(3), PaiChecker introduces a two-level self-correction mechanism: Phase II re-verifies each label against its textual evidence, and Phase III validates it against the actual code implementation. We evaluate PaiChecker on SWE-Gym [32] and SWE-bench Multilingual [29], comparing it against three prompting baselines, and four agent-framework baselines. We identify PR-Issue misalignment as a systematic construction problem in SWE-bench-like benchmarks. Empirical Study. We analyze all 500 SWE-bench Verified instances, deriving a taxonomy of five patterns with 11 scenarios and finding 13.6% misaligned (Section 2). Detection Framework. We propose PaiChecker, a multi-agent framework for automated detection and categorization of PRIssue misalignment (Section 3). Evaluation. testCases.input: Examine the distinctions between PaiChecker's methodology and SWE-bench Verified in addressing PR-Issue misalignment.
testCases.actualOutput:
PaiChecker and SWE-bench Verified address PR-Issue misalignment through different methodologies and objectives. 

SWE-bench Verified serves as a benchmark that includes a human-validated subset of instances, focusing on providing a high-quality baseline for evaluating software engineering (SE) benchmarks. It emphasizes the importance of human validation to ensure that misalignments identified in this dataset reflect broader issues in similar benchmarks. The dataset comprises 500 instances, and the validation process is crucial for establishing a reliable foundation for subsequent analyses and evaluations [2. arXiv:2607.28587v1].

In contrast, PaiChecker is a multi-agent framework specifically designed to detect and categorize PR-Issue misalignment systematically. It operates through a three-phase methodology: 

1. **Phase I** focuses on specific misalignment identification using three specialized subagents that analyze different aspects of the PR and issue artifacts.
2. **Phase II** synthesizes the outputs from Phase I into preliminary labels and rationales, while also allowing for the assignment of an "Others" category.
3. **Phase III** employs a code validator to cross-reference textual judgments against actual code implementations, filtering out false positives that may arise from textual reasoning alone [1. arXiv:2607.28587v1; 3. arXiv:2607.28587v1].

While SWE-bench Verified provides a foundational dataset for evaluating misalignments, PaiChecker actively identifies and categorizes these misalignments through a structured, multi-phase approach. This allows PaiChecker to achieve high accuracy rates (up to 92.12% and 91.67% on different datasets) in detecting misalignments, demonstrating its effectiveness in addressing the systematic issues that undermine evaluation fairness and reliability in software engineering benchmarks [4. arXiv:2607.28587v1; 9. arXiv:2607.28587v1]. 

In summary, SWE-bench Verified lays the groundwork for understanding misalignments, while PaiChecker provides a robust mechanism for detecting and categorizing these issues in a scalable manner.

PaiChecker and SWE-bench Verified differ significantly in their approaches to addressing PR-Issue misalignment. 

1. **Methodology**: PaiChecker employs a three-phase multi-agent system that includes pattern-specific detection, cross-agent label synthesis, and code validation. This allows for a more comprehensive and scalable detection of misalignments. In contrast, SWE-bench Verified relies on a standard construction pipeline that assumes PRs are well-aligned with their linked issues, which is often not the case.

2. **Detection of Misalignment**: PaiChecker systematically identifies misalignments across five patterns and eleven scenarios, revealing a 13.6% misalignment rate in its analysis of 500 instances. SWE-bench Verified does not have a dedicated mechanism for identifying these misalignments, leading to potential evaluation fairness issues.

3. **Performance**: PaiChecker has demonstrated high accuracy rates of up to 92.12% and 91.67% on SWE-Gym and SWE-bench Multilingual, respectively, indicating its effectiveness in detecting misalignment. SWE-bench Verified lacks such performance metrics as it does not focus on misalignment detection.

Overall, PaiChecker provides a more robust framework for identifying and addressing PR-Issue misalignment compared to the assumptions made by SWE-bench Verified.

SWE-bench-like Benchmarks. SWE-bench [29] introduced real-world GitHub issue resolution as an LLM evaluation paradigm, spawning many derivatives. Other variants, including SWE-PolyBench [35], SWE-Perf [27], SWE-Bench++ [40], SWE-Evo [39], SWE-Fixer [45], SWE-Flow [53], SWE-Universe [22], and SWE-Lego [37], extend the paradigm along other dimensions.
Benchmark Quality and Reliability. Benchmark reliability is a longstanding concern, with prior work highlighting test oracle insufficiency [42, 51], dataset contamination [14], and solution leakage [15]. This paper identifies PR-Issue misalignment as a systematic construction-level problem in SWE-bench-like benchmarks that directly undermines evaluation fairness and reliability. Manual analysis of all 500 SWE-bench Verified instances reveals 13.6% misalign- ment across five patterns and 11 fine-grained scenarios. Section: 2.1 Study Design

2.1.1 Dataset. We conduct our study on SWE-bench Verified [23], a human-validated subset of 500 SWE-Bench [29] instances. We select it for two reasons: (1) its human validation represents a high-quality baseline, so misalignments found here likely reflect broader issues in other SWE-bench-like benchmarks; (2) its official experiments repository [2] provides per-instance resolution data for 131 leaderboard agents, enabling quantitative analysis for RQ2.
2.1.2 Method. Manual Examination Process. Following established practices in qualitative SE research [18, 24], we apply open coding [36] to derive a misalignment taxonomy (RQ1). First, we collect per instance: issue-side artifacts (description, discussion), PR-side artifacts (description, discussion, code review, commits, changed files), and cross-reference metadata. Then, we code all 500 instances, iteratively grouping codes into higher-level categories to form a draft taxonomy; a single instance may exhibit multiple patterns. Last, the draft taxonomy was reviewed by the second author; disagreements were resolved with a third author until consensus.
Leaderboard Data Collection. To assess the impact of misalignment on evaluation reliability, we collect per-instance resolution data from the official SWE-bench experiments repository [2], recording per-instance resolution counts for 131 leaderboard agents.

Section: 4.1 Evaluation Dataset

We evaluate on two datasets disjoint from our preliminary study: SWE-Gym[32](2,438 Python tasks) and SWE-bench Multilingual [29] (300 tasks covering C, C++, Go, Java, JavaScript/TypeScript, PHP, Ruby, and Rust). Selection followed five criteria: (i) SWE-bench-style automated PR-Issue pairing; (ii) no manual specification rewriting, so raw defects remain observable; (iii) feasible for full manual annotation yet sufficiently large; (iv) multi-repo and widely adopted; and (v) PR identifiers available for full-content access. Two annotators with development experience independently labeled all instances following our taxonomy (Section 2.2.1), guided by structured questions adapted from SWE-bench annotation instructions [1]. They achieved Cohen's Kappa [33] of 𝜅 = 0 . 91 on binary judgment and 𝜅 = 0 . 86 on fine-grained labeling; disagreements were resolved by a third author. Table 2 summarizes the dataset statistics.
Misalignment rates differ across datasets: 13.6% in SWE-bench Verified (Table 1), 44.3% in SWE-Gym, and 24.3% in SWE-bench Multilingual, largely reflecting SWE-bench Verified's human curation. Patterns tied to underspecification and test coverage drop most sharply in Verified: UL decreases from 15.9% (SWE-Gym) and 3.0% (Multilingual) to 0.2%, IS from 14.0% and 4.3% to 3.6%, and SC from 17.6% and 11.0% to 4.4%. In contrast, deeper PR-Issue relationship defects remain comparable: DP stays near 6.0-8.0%, and FP remains low across all three datasets (0.6%, 4.5%, 0.7%). These defects are harder to infer from the task alone and thus more likely to escape human curation.

Section: 3.1 Phase I: Specific Misalignment Identification

In this subsection, we describe Phase I, which detects the five misalignment patterns using three parallel subagents, each focused on distinct reasoning: the Issue Analyzer targets Incomplete Specification (IS), primarily drawing on issue-side artifacts; the PR Scope Analyzer targets PR Scope Creep (SC) and Unspecified Literal (UL) through issue-versus-PR scope comparison; and the PR Connection Analyzer targets Defective PR (DP) and Follow-up PR (FP) through temporal cross-PR reasoning. This grouping keeps each subagent's context compact and reasoning focused. All three produce a uniform structured output: (i) a judgment per target pattern, (ii) supporting evidence for text-level self-correction, and (iii) suspicious clues -anomalies outside the subagent's target patterns that support beyond-taxonomy generalization.
3.1.1 Issue Analyzer. The Issue Analyzer operationalizes IS detection by comparing the issue description against its discussion thread. As mentioned in Section 2.2.1: a well-formed bug report comprises three key components: reproduction code, actual behavior, and expected behavior. Based on this, the subagent performs two checks.
First, whether the issue is incomplete: it identifies whether a maintainer explicitly requests the reporter to supplement any of these components, grounding the judgment in community consensus rather than subjective assessment. Second, whether the issue has been redefined: it checks whether any of these components differs between the original description and the discussion; a change in any component signals that the addressed problem has shifted.
3.1.2 PR Scope Analyzer. The PR Scope Analyzer detects SC and UL in a unified pass. Both patterns require establishing the issue's requested scope as a baseline and checking whether the PR exceeds it, so a single subagent establishes the baseline once and verifies both patterns together. This subagent receives the issue description as scope baseline, PR-side text for what the PR claims to deliver, and both patches for UL detection.
Following the text-driven, code-validation principle, SC is triggered only when PR-side textual artifacts explicitly claim work beyond the issue's scope. UL is triggered when all three conditions hold: (1) the test patch asserts a hardcoded literal ( e.g. a string, number, or exception message); (2) the literal is newly added in the code patch as a fixed constant, rather than read from existing metadata; and (3) it does not appear verbatim in the issue description.
3.1.3 PR Connection Analyzer. The PR Connection Analyzer detects DP and FP, both involve temporal relationships between the current PR and other PRs for the same issue. Tracing such crossPR dependency chains requires information beyond the current instance's artifacts, so we equip this subagent with GitHub API access to actively search for and retrieve related PRs.

For DP detection, the agent searches for PRs merged after the current one that still address the same issue. Each candidate is verified for merge status to distinguish corrective follow-ups from unrelated references. For FP detection, the agent searches for earlier merged PRs that partially addressed the same issue, checking whether the current PR is a supplementary contribution rather than an independent fix, based on merge chronology and follow-up language in PR descriptions.

Section: 4.3 Evaluation Metrics

We evaluate PR-Issue misalignment detection from two complementary perspectives: (1) a binary classification task that judges whether an instance is aligned or misaligned, and (2) a multilabel classification task that identifies the specific misalignment patterns, where an instance may exhibit multiple patterns simultaneously. Accordingly, we adopt the following metrics:
Binary Detection. We measure accuracy, precision, recall, and F1 for the binary detection task.
Multi-Class Categorization. Exact Match (EM) serves as the primary metric, requiring the predicted label set to exactly match the ground truth. We supplement EM with macro-averaged accuracy, precision, recall, and F1. For per-label analysis, we report only F1 due to space constraints; F1 provides a balanced measure of precision and recall, making it sufficient for diagnostic purposes.

Section: 4.4 Backbone LLMs

We evaluate PaiChecker and baselines across four state-of-the-art LLM backbones, including three closed-source models GPT-5.3Codex [31], Claude-Sonnet-4.6 [16], Gemini-3.1-Pro-Preview [26], and one open-sourced model Qwen-3.5-Plus [34]. All models were accessed through their respective APIs.

testCases.input: What are the defining characteristics and constraints of ILP-GT in voter interval contexts?
testCases.actualOutput:
The Integer Linear Program for Generalized Thiele (ILP-GT) in the context of Voter Interval (VI) preferences has specific defining characteristics and constraints that facilitate its formulation and solution. 

In a VI context, the approval profile is structured such that for each candidate \( c \in C \), the set of voters who approve \( c \) forms a consecutive segment on a linear order of voters. This property allows for a systematic approach to defining the candidates' support, where each candidate's supporters can be represented as intervals. The formulation of ILP-GT is designed to maximize the total score based on these intervals, ensuring that the selected committee of candidates reflects the preferences of the voters effectively.

One key aspect of ILP-GT is its reliance on a constraint matrix that is not totally unimodular (TU) when dealing with VI preferences. This is significant because, while total unimodularity allows for polynomial-time solutions, the structure of the VI approval profile can lead to matrices that do not retain this property. For instance, the addition of an all-ones row to the approval matrix may disrupt the consecutive ones property, resulting in a non-TU matrix, which complicates the solution process [1].

To address these challenges, the ILP-GT formulation can be modified. For example, if all candidates are approved by exactly two voters, the constraints can be adjusted to ensure that the responsibility for enforcing committee size is shifted from candidate selection variables to voter satisfaction variables. This adjustment helps in transforming the ILP-GT into a generalized matching matrix, which can then be solved in polynomial time [2].

Overall, the defining characteristics of ILP-GT in the VI context revolve around the structured representation of voter preferences and the careful management of constraints to facilitate efficient computation, despite the inherent complexities introduced by the non-TU nature of the approval profiles.

1. **Approval Profiles**: The approval profile can be either Condorcet Interval (CI) or Voter Interval (VI). CI profiles maintain total unimodularity (TU), allowing for polynomial-time solutions, while VI profiles may not preserve TU when an all-ones row is appended.

2. **Variables**: The model includes variables \(y_c\) that indicate selected candidates and \(x_{v,i}\) that track voter satisfaction levels.

3. **Constraints**: The formulation includes constraints that ensure the selection of candidates aligns with voter approvals. In the case of CI, the constraints maintain the consecutive ones property, while for VI, this property may be lost, complicating the solution.

4. **Committee Size**: The original constraint ensuring exactly \(k\) candidates are selected is modified to shift responsibility to the voter satisfaction variables, ensuring that each candidate selected corresponds to two approving voters.

5. **Generalized Matching Matrix**: The modified ILP-GT formulation results in a generalized matching matrix, which allows for polynomial-time solvability under specific conditions regarding the coefficients of the constraint matrix.

6. **FPT Parameterization**: The problem is FPT (Fixed Parameter Tractable) parameterized by \( \Delta C + \Delta V \), indicating that it can be solved efficiently when the parameters related to candidate and voter diversity are bounded.

These characteristics and constraints define how ILP-GT operates within the voter interval context, influencing both its complexity and solvability.

Section: 1 Introduction Multi-winner elections based on approval ballots are used in many settings, such as recommendation systems, committee selection, and blockchain [SFL16, LS23, BBC + 24], where every voter expresses its preferences as a subset of candidates it approves of. A central family of voting rules for such applications are Thiele rules [Thi95], which include Proportional Approval Voting (PAV) as a prominent member [AGG + 15]. These rules balance diversity, proportionality, and excellence in the selected committee, depending on the specific Thiele rule used [LS21]. For instance, ChamberlinCourant Approval Voting (CC) [CC83] promotes diversity by ensuring broad representation; PAV aims for proportional representation, satisfying strong proportionality axioms like EJR+ [BP23]; Multi-winner Approval Voting focuses on excellence by selecting the most approved candidates. However, computing a winning committee under Thiele rules is computationally challenging. In fact, finding a winning committee under any non-trivial Thiele rule (i.e., every rule except for Multi-winner Approval Voting) is NP-hard. For CC and PAV, the problems remain NP-hard even ∗ A conference version of this work appeared in AAAI 2026 [LS26]. Krzysztof Sornat AGH University, Poland sornat@agh.edu.pl under very restricted conditions where each candidate is approved by exactly 3 voters and each voter approves exactly 2 candidates [AGG + 15, SFL16]. 1 In the CI domain, candidates can be ordered so that each voter's approval set forms a contiguous interval. CI captures scenarios where candidates are linearly ordered, e.g. by ideology or location, and each voter is focused on a specific region of the spectrum. One key advantage of CI is that it allows the winner determination problem for all Thiele rules to be solved efficiently. It is by using an integer linear programming formulation that admits a totally unimodular constraint matrix, which are known to be solvable in polynomial time [Pet18, PL20]. To better understand and overcome this computational hardness, a natural direction is to restrict the input domain. Such restrictions often enable polynomial-time algorithms for otherwise intractable rules, and this approach has been particularly fruitful in approval-based committee elections. Two central restricted domains for approval ballots are the Candidate Interval (CI) and the Voter Interval (VI) domains [ELP17, ELP25]. The VI domain, in contrast, imposes structure on the voters rather than on the candidates. Here, voters can be ordered so that each candidate is approved by a consecutive segment of voters. This domain models scenarios where voters are structured by demographic or socioeconomic features such as age, income, or education level, and candidates appeal to specific groups, e.g. young voters, low-income households, or university-educated individuals. The VI domain has received significant attention [ELP17, ELP25] and, consequently, for several voting rules, such as CC, Monroe's and Minimax Approval Voting polynomial-time winner-determination algorithms for VI elections are known [BSU13, LG16]. Yet, for most Thiele rules, and PAV in particular, the computational complexity of winner determination on VI remains a prominent open question [ELP17, Pet18, GBSF21, LS23, ELP25]. Despite the dual nature of the VI and CI domains, the techniques used for CI do not translate to VI. In particular, the constraint matrix of the integer linear programming formulation is not totally unimodular anymore under VI preferences and, thus, it is not clear whether this problem can be solved in polynomial time or not. testCases.name: test_case_37
testCases.input: How does the total unimodularity of ILP-GT's constraint matrix influence CI approval profiles?
testCases.actualOutput:
The total unimodularity (TU) of the constraint matrix in the Integer Linear Programming formulation for Generalized Thiele (ILP-GT) plays a crucial role in the efficiency of solving election problems under Candidate Interval (CI) approval profiles. When the approval profile is CI, the constraint matrix of ILP-GT is TU, which implies that an optimal solution can be found in polynomial time.

As noted in the excerpts, Peters [Pet18] demonstrated that the TU property is maintained when the approval profile is CI, due to the consecutive one property inherent in CI profiles. This property allows for the formulation of the ILP-GT to be structured in such a way that the matrix remains totally unimodular even when an additional row (such as a cardinality constraint) is appended. Specifically, the matrix retains its TU status because the additional row consists solely of 1s, which aligns with the consecutive 1s property of CI profiles. Consequently, this ensures that the ILP can be solved efficiently, leading to polynomial-time algorithms for determining winning committees under Thiele rules in CI contexts [1. arXiv:2607.28575v1].

In contrast, when the approval profile is not CI, such as in Voter Interval (VI) profiles, the TU property may not hold. This loss of total unimodularity complicates the computational landscape, making it unclear whether the problem can still be solved in polynomial time [3. arXiv:2607.28575v1]. Thus, the total unimodularity of the ILP-GT's constraint matrix is a key factor that facilitates efficient computation in CI approval profiles, while its absence in other profiles poses significant challenges.

Section: 1 Introduction Multi-winner elections based on approval ballots are used in many settings, such as recommendation systems, committee selection, and blockchain [SFL16, LS23, BBC + 24], where every voter expresses its preferences as a subset of candidates it approves of. A central family of voting rules for such applications are Thiele rules [Thi95], which include Proportional Approval Voting (PAV) as a prominent member [AGG + 15]. These rules balance diversity, proportionality, and excellence in the selected committee, depending on the specific Thiele rule used [LS21]. For instance, ChamberlinCourant Approval Voting (CC) [CC83] promotes diversity by ensuring broad representation; PAV aims for proportional representation, satisfying strong proportionality axioms like EJR+ [BP23]; Multi-winner Approval Voting focuses on excellence by selecting the most approved candidates. However, computing a winning committee under Thiele rules is computationally challenging. In fact, finding a winning committee under any non-trivial Thiele rule (i.e., every rule except for Multi-winner Approval Voting) is NP-hard. For CC and PAV, the problems remain NP-hard even ∗ A conference version of this work appeared in AAAI 2026 [LS26]. CI captures scenarios where candidates are linearly ordered, e.g. by ideology or location, and each voter is focused on a specific region of the spectrum. One key advantage of CI is that it allows the winner determination problem for all Thiele rules to be solved efficiently. It is by using an integer linear programming formulation that admits a totally unimodular constraint matrix, which are known to be solvable in polynomial time [Pet18, PL20]. To better understand and overcome this computational hardness, a natural direction is to restrict the input domain. Such restrictions often enable polynomial-time algorithms for otherwise intractable rules, and this approach has been particularly fruitful in approval-based committee elections. Two central restricted domains for approval ballots are the Candidate Interval (CI) and the Voter Interval (VI) domains [ELP17, ELP25]. The VI domain, in contrast, imposes structure on the voters rather than on the candidates. Here, voters can be ordered so that each candidate is approved by a consecutive segment of voters. This domain models scenarios where voters are structured by demographic or socioeconomic features such as age, income, or education level, and candidates appeal to specific groups, e.g. young voters, low-income households, or university-educated individuals. The VI domain has received significant attention [ELP17, ELP25] and, consequently, for several voting rules, such as CC, Monroe's and Minimax Approval Voting polynomial-time winner-determination algorithms for VI elections are known [BSU13, LG16]. Yet, for most Thiele rules, and PAV in particular, the computational complexity of winner determination on VI remains a prominent open question [ELP17, Pet18, GBSF21, LS23, ELP25]. This work takes a new approach to understand the computational complexity of Thiele rules by studying the structure of winning committees. Instead of considering candidates in isolation, we examine how shared support among voters constrains the possible combinations of candidates in a winning committee. We provide a structural characterization of optimal committees under Thiele rules based on a dominance relation among candidates. Specifically, a candidate c is said to dominate another candidate d if the set of supporters of c strictly contains that of d . This induces a hierarchy of dominancy levels where candidates within the same level do not dominate one another and each is dominated by some candidate in a higher level. We show that there always exists a winning committee that is non-dominated , meaning that no member is dominated by any candidate outside the committee. These structural insights apply to general approval profiles and are of independent interest, offering new theoretical tools for analyzing and determining winners under Thiele rules. Practically, this structure can guide the development of more efficient algorithms and heuristics. Theoretically, it offers a new perspective on the open question of whether winner determination under PAV is polynomial-time solvable on VI. 2 Algorithmic Results. We show that our structural insights are particularly effective when combined with the VI property: candidates of a VI instance can be partitioned into parts such that candidates within a part influence only a limited number of voters. This allows to design a dynamic program over a sequence of such parts, exploiting the limited interaction. As a result, we obtain an FPT algorithm for PAV and, more generally, for any Thiele rule, when parameterized by two parameters combined: the maximum number of approvals received by a candidate, and the maximum number of approvals in a vote. Notably, the same parameterization is para-NP-hard in the general (unstructured) case-that is, the problem remains NP-hard even when both parameters are constants. testCases.input: What does the reduction of Generalized Thiele to p-partial set cover reveal about its FPT parameterization by k + ∆C?
testCases.actualOutput:
The reduction of Generalized Thiele to the p-partial set cover problem reveals that Generalized Thiele is fixed-parameter tractable (FPT) when parameterized by \( k + \Delta_C \). This is significant because it demonstrates that the complexity of solving Generalized Thiele can be managed effectively by focusing on these parameters.

In the reduction, the problem is framed such that voters are treated as elements in a universe, while candidates correspond to sets of voters that approve them. The goal is to cover at least \( p \) different elements (voters) using a minimal number of candidate sets. The reduction leverages the fact that any \( k \) candidates can satisfy at most \( k \cdot \Delta_C \) different voters, allowing the parameter \( p \) to be bounded by \( k \) and \( \Delta_C \) [1. arXiv:2607.28575v1].

The authors utilize color coding to manage the approvals in a way that reflects their contributions to the objective function. Each approval is colored to indicate its additive contribution, which allows for a more nuanced representation of how candidates cover voters. This coloring helps ensure that the optimal solution can be identified efficiently, as it allows the algorithm to simulate the necessary coverage while maintaining the integrity of the objective function [2. arXiv:2607.28575v1].

The overall running time of the resulting FPT algorithm is influenced by these parameters, leading to a time complexity of \( 2^{O(k \cdot k! \Delta_C)} \cdot n \cdot m \), which is manageable given the constraints of \( k \) and \( \Delta_C \) [3. arXiv:2607.28575v1]. Thus, the reduction not only establishes the FPT nature of Generalized Thiele but also provides a structured approach to solving it efficiently under specific conditions.

testCases.actualOutput:
The FPT (Fixed Parameter Tractable) algorithm for Generalized Thiele, parameterized by \( k + \Delta_C \), has significant implications for structured elections and combinatorial optimization. This algorithm effectively reduces the Generalized Thiele problem to a variant of the set cover problem known as the \( p \)-partial set cover, where the goal is to cover at least \( p \) distinct elements from a universe using a minimal number of subsets. The reduction is particularly beneficial because the \( p \)-partial set cover problem is known to be FPT time solvable when parameterized by \( p \) [1].
